boomi: Boomi is an enterprise integration and automation platform used to connect applications, APIs, databases, files, events and data across cloud and on-premises environments. | Capabilities: Provides integration process design, connectors, APIs, runtime infrastructure, data transformation, B2B/EDI, master data and monitoring capabilities. | Interview Context: I describe Boomi as an iPaaS platform that reduces point-to-point integration by providing reusable processes, connectors and centrally managed deployment and monitoring.
ipaas: Integration Platform as a Service is a cloud-based integration approach that provides managed tooling and runtime capabilities for connecting applications and data. | Capabilities: Typically includes connectors, orchestration, transformation, API integration, monitoring and deployment management. | Interview Context: Boomi is an iPaaS because it provides a platform for designing, deploying, executing and monitoring integrations without building the entire integration infrastructure from scratch.
component: A reusable Boomi configuration object used to build, configure or support an integration. | Capabilities: Components include processes, profiles, maps, connections, operations, properties, certificates, cross reference tables and other platform assets. | Interview Context: I think of a component as a building block that can be reused or referenced by one or more integration processes.
process: A Boomi process is the executable integration workflow that defines how documents are received, transformed, routed and delivered. | Capabilities: A process is built from steps such as Start, Connector, Map, Decision, Route, Flow Control, Try/Catch and Process Call. | Interview Context: I normally explain a process from the business flow first: receive data, validate it, transform it, call the target and handle success or failure.
execution: An execution is a running instance of a Boomi process. | Capabilities: It represents a particular runtime execution and has execution status, timing, logs and document activity associated with it. | Interview Context: When troubleshooting production, I start with the execution record because it gives me the process, runtime, timing and failure information needed to isolate the issue.
profile: A profile defines the structure or layout of data processed by a Boomi integration. | Capabilities: Profiles can represent XML, JSON, flat files, databases, EDI and other structured formats, including fields, hierarchy, data types and delimiters. | Interview Context: I use profiles to tell Boomi what the incoming or outgoing document looks like so that connectors and maps can process it correctly.
connection: A Connection defines how Boomi connects to an external system or technology endpoint. | Capabilities: It normally contains endpoint information, credentials, authentication and transport-level configuration, while the Operation defines what action is performed. | Interview Context: A simple interview explanation is Connection answers 'where and how do I connect?' and Operation answers 'what do I do after connecting?'.
operation: An Operation defines the action and data structure used by a connector. | Capabilities: It specifies actions such as query, get, create, update, delete, read or write and commonly contains request/response profile information. | Interview Context: I create or reuse an Operation according to the business action required, while keeping endpoint and authentication details in the Connection.
connector: A Boomi connector is the integration interface used to communicate with an application, database, protocol or technology. | Capabilities: Connectors expose Connection and Operation components and abstract protocol-specific implementation details. | Interview Context: I select a connector based on the target technology, then configure its Connection and Operation and place the connector shape in the process.
connector_connection_vs_operation: Connection and Operation are complementary connector components. | Connection: Holds endpoint, credentials, authentication and transport configuration. | Operation: Defines the action, object and request/response structure. | Interview Context: For example, in SFTP the Connection can contain host and authentication, while the Operation defines Read, Write, List, Listen or Delete.
document: A document is the unit of data that flows through a Boomi process. | Capabilities: A document carries payload data plus associated document metadata and properties as it moves through process steps. | Interview Context: I distinguish a document from a process execution: one execution can process many documents, and each document can take a different path based on routing or errors.
document_tracking: Document tracking is the ability to associate business or technical identifiers with documents so individual records can be located during monitoring. | Capabilities: Tracking can use document properties and connector tracking fields to make production support easier. | Interview Context: I normally expose a correlation ID, order ID, customer ID or source file name as a tracking value when the business needs record-level troubleshooting.
runtime: A Boomi Runtime is the execution engine where integration processes actually run. | Capabilities: It provides the JVM-based execution environment, local resources, connectivity and processing needed to execute deployed processes. | Interview Context: I separate design-time platform services from runtime execution: the platform manages components and deployments, while the runtime executes the integration.
basic runtime: A basic runtime is a single-tenant, single-node runtime engine. | Capabilities: It executes deployed processes on one node and is suitable when the workload and availability requirements do not justify a cluster. | Interview Context: I would use a basic runtime for simpler or lower-volume integrations, but I would evaluate a runtime cluster for mission-critical high-availability workloads.
runtime cluster: A Runtime Cluster is a single-tenant, multi-node runtime engine. | Capabilities: Multiple nodes work as a logical runtime, distributing executions and improving availability and capacity. | Interview Context: For a mission-critical enterprise integration with high volume or availability requirements, I would use a Runtime Cluster so one node failure does not necessarily stop the whole integration workload.
atom: The Atom is Boomi's lightweight, single-tenant runtime engine that executes integration processes locally behind corporate firewalls or inside private cloud VPCs. | Capabilities: Executes scheduled or listener-based integration processes; manages local disk caching and in-memory queueing; supports both on-premise and private cloud deployments with minimal infrastructure footprint; auto-updates to the latest platform version without manual intervention. | Interview Context: The Atom is your go-to when you need to integrate with systems sitting behind a firewall — like an on-premise SAP or Oracle database. It's a single point of failure though, so for anything mission-critical or high-volume, you'd move up to a Molecule. Think of it as the 'lite' runtime — perfect for dev environments, small batch jobs, or scenarios where you absolutely cannot expose data to the cloud.
molecule: A Molecule is Boomi's clustered, single-tenant runtime engine that provides high availability and horizontal scalability by distributing execution across multiple server nodes. | Capabilities: Load-balances process executions across multiple nodes sharing a common file system (typically NFS); automatically redistributes work if a head node fails; supports forked execution for process isolation; enables parallel processing across JVMs; scales horizontally by adding worker nodes. | Interview Context: This is the standard enterprise deployment pattern. If you're running 500,000+ documents per day or have SLA-backed integrations, you need a Molecule. The head node coordinates, worker nodes execute. If one node goes down, the others pick up the load. On AWS or Azure, you'd typically deploy Molecules across availability zones with shared EFS/Azure Files storage.
atom cloud: An Atom Cloud is Boomi's multi-tenant, highly scalable runtime infrastructure hosted and managed by Boomi or certified partners. | Capabilities: Uses forked execution isolation per tenant account ensuring complete resource and security separation; zero local infrastructure maintenance required; auto-scales worker nodes based on demand; supports both Boomi-hosted and private runtime clouds (customer-managed worker pools); ideal for pure cloud-to-cloud integrations. | Interview Context: When you don't want to manage any infrastructure, Atom Cloud is the answer. Salesforce-to-NetSuite, Workday-to-SAP SuccessFactors — these pure SaaS integrations thrive here. Each tenant gets their own forked JVM, so even though it's multi-tenant, your processes are isolated. For regulated industries, you can deploy a Private Atom Cloud where Boomi manages the control plane but your workers run in your VPC.
forked execution: Forked Execution is Boomi's security and resource isolation mechanism that spawns a dedicated JVM for each process execution rather than running inside the shared head node JVM. | Capabilities: Prevents memory leaks, thread starvation, and runaway processes from crashing the entire cluster; isolates tenant processes in multi-tenant Cloud environments; configurable heap size and JVM arguments per forked process; critical for high-concurrency and multi-tenant deployments. | Interview Context: This is what makes Atom Clouds safe for multi-tenant use. Without forked execution, one badly written process with a memory leak could bring down every other process on that node. In interviews, mention that you configure forked execution properties via the Runtime Configuration APIs — things like min/max heap, permgen size, and garbage collection flags. It's the difference between a stable production environment and 3 AM pages.
jvm: JVM is the Java Virtual Machine in which Boomi runtime code executes. | Capabilities: It manages heap memory, threads and Java application execution. | Interview Context: JVM awareness matters when diagnosing high memory usage, garbage collection pressure, thread starvation or out-of-memory errors.
heap: Heap is the JVM-managed memory area used by Java objects during execution. | Capabilities: Boomi processes consume heap for documents, transformations, maps and runtime objects, and garbage collection reclaims unused objects. | Interview Context: Large documents, high concurrency and inefficient transformations can increase heap pressure, so I look at volume, concurrency and document size when diagnosing memory problems.
node: A node is one runtime JVM participating in a runtime cluster or cloud. | Capabilities: Multiple nodes can collectively provide execution capacity and availability. | Interview Context: In a clustered deployment, I think about the node as the individual worker unit and the cluster as the logical runtime presented to management.
high availability: High Availability means designing the integration platform so service remains available despite expected component or node failures. | Capabilities: Runtime clusters, redundant infrastructure and resilient downstream communication can reduce single points of failure. | Interview Context: I would explain HA as an architecture property rather than a single Boomi shape: multiple runtime nodes, resilient dependencies and controlled failure handling are all part of it.
load balancing: Load balancing distributes execution workload across available runtime nodes or processing threads. | Capabilities: It prevents one execution node from becoming the sole processing bottleneck in a clustered architecture. | Interview Context: I use clustered runtime capacity and appropriate process-level parallelism to increase throughput, while checking downstream limits before increasing concurrency.
failover: Failover is the ability to continue service or processing when a runtime node or infrastructure component becomes unavailable. | Capabilities: Runtime clusters can provide alternative execution capacity when individual nodes fail. | Interview Context: I distinguish failover from retry: failover changes where processing can run, while retry repeats a failed operation or document.
start shape: The Start Shape is the entry point of every Boomi process that defines how and when the process is triggered. | Capabilities: Connector-triggered (real-time listener); Schedule-triggered (cron-based); No Data (manual/test execution); Test mode with sample data; supports multiple start shapes in a single process for different trigger types. | Interview Context: The Start Shape is where execution begins. If you're building a REST API, the Start Shape is a Connector listening on the Shared Web Server. If you're doing a nightly batch sync, it's a Schedule shape set to run at 2 AM. The No Data shape is for testing — you can manually kick off a process without any input. In real projects, you rarely use multiple start shapes in one process; it's cleaner to have separate processes for different trigger patterns.
connector shape: The Connector Shape is the bridge between Boomi processes and external systems — it sends data to or receives data from applications, databases, files, and APIs. | Capabilities: Supports all connector types (Application, Technology, Event-driven); configurable connection and operation components; handles authentication, encryption, and protocol negotiation; manages connection pooling and retry logic; supports both request and listen modes. | Interview Context: The Connector Shape is the workhorse of any integration. You drag it onto the canvas, select your pre-built Connection (the 'where'), and your Operation (the 'what'). For a Database connector, the Connection has the JDBC URL and credentials; the Operation has the SQL query. For HTTP Client, the Connection has the base URL; the Operation has the GET/POST/PUT/PATH and endpoint path. Understanding that Connection and Operation are separate, reusable components is fundamental.
map shape: The Map Shape is Boomi's core data transformation engine that converts source data profiles into target data profiles using field-to-field mappings, functions, and lookups. | Capabilities: Maps between XML, JSON, Flat File, Database, and EDI profiles; supports standard mapping functions (string, date, math, logic); allows custom Groovy/JavaScript functions; performs Document Cache lookups for enrichment; handles 1-to-1, 1-to-many, and many-to-1 transformations; supports profile caching for performance. | Interview Context: This is where the magic happens. You have a Salesforce Account JSON on the left and a SAP Customer XML on the right — the Map Shape bridges them. You drag fields from source to target, apply functions like 'To Upper Case' or 'Date Format,' and do cache lookups for reference data. Best practice: use standard Map Functions over custom scripting whenever possible. A Map with 50 standard functions is maintainable; a Map with one giant Groovy script is a maintenance nightmare. Also, for large lookups, always use Document Cache instead of repeated database calls.
data process: Data Process is a general-purpose process step for manipulating documents or data before or after other integration steps. | Capabilities: It can support operations such as splitting, combining, searching/replacing, encoding/decoding and other document-level processing depending on configuration. | Interview Context: I use Data Process when the requirement is document manipulation rather than a full source-to-target mapping.
decision shape: The Decision Shape is a conditional router that evaluates document content against defined criteria and routes documents down different paths based on the result. | Capabilities: Evaluates simple or compound conditions (AND/OR logic); supports comparison operators (equals, contains, greater than, etc.); routes documents to True or False branches; can evaluate document properties, profile elements, or dynamic properties; supports nested decisions for complex logic. | Interview Context: Decision is your if/else logic. 'If OrderAmount > 10000, route to HighValue branch; else route to Standard branch.' Each document is evaluated individually, so in a batch of 1000, maybe 50 go left and 950 go right. Common use case: routing error documents to a retry queue vs. a dead letter queue. For complex nested logic (if A and B or C and not D), consider using a Business Rules shape or a Data Process script instead of 5 nested Decisions.
route shape: The Route Shape is a content-based router that evaluates documents against multiple conditions and sends each document to exactly one matching path. | Capabilities: Supports multiple routing conditions with priority ordering; evaluates document properties, profile fields, or dynamic properties; sends documents to the first matching route; supports a default/fallback route for non-matching documents; more efficient than multiple chained Decision shapes. | Interview Context: Route is like a switch statement. 'If Region = US, send to US_Queue; if Region = EU, send to EU_Queue; else send to Default_Queue.' Unlike Branch (which sends copies everywhere), Route sends each document to exactly one destination. This is the right choice when you have 3+ possible destinations. For just two paths, Decision is simpler.
branch shape: The Branch Shape creates parallel execution paths within a process, allowing documents to flow down multiple branches simultaneously. | Capabilities: Splits a single document stream into multiple independent paths; each branch executes in parallel within the same JVM; supports conditional branching based on document content; documents from all branches reunite at a Join shape; useful for parallel API calls or independent transformations. | Interview Context: Branch is for parallelism, not decision-making. If you need to call three different APIs with the same input data, Branch lets you do it simultaneously instead of sequentially. But be careful — each branch gets a copy of the document, so if you have 10,000 documents and 3 branches, you're now processing 30,000 document instances. Memory planning is critical. Also, branches reunite automatically at the next shape after the branch block.
flow control: The Flow Control Shape manages process execution throttling and parallelism, allowing you to split document batches into configurable threads or multi-node workers. | Capabilities: Parallel Processing mode distributes documents across multiple threads or Molecule nodes; Sequential Processing mode forces one document at a time; configurable thread count and batch size; supports both local JVM threads and distributed Molecule node processing; throttling to prevent downstream system overload. | Interview Context: Flow Control is your throughput knob. For a database load, you might set 10 threads with 500-document batches to maximize throughput. For an API with strict rate limits (say, 100 requests/minute), you set 1 thread with 1-document batches. In a Molecule, Parallel Processing can distribute work across nodes — so 4 nodes with 10 threads each gives you 40 concurrent execution paths. But beware: more threads means more memory and more database connections. Always monitor connection pool exhaustion.
try catch: The Try Catch Shape is a document-level error handling construct that catches failures on individual documents and routes them to a Catch branch while allowing successful documents to continue downstream. | Capabilities: Catches All Errors or specifically Document Errors; routes failed documents to the Catch branch; allows successful documents to proceed on the Try branch; supports nested Try Catch blocks; can capture error messages, stack traces, and document content; essential for dead-letter queuing patterns. | Interview Context: This is what prevents one bad apple from spoiling the bunch. If you're processing 10,000 CSV records and record #5,432 has a malformed date, Try Catch catches that one record, sends it to the Catch branch for logging/retry, and the other 9,999 records continue normally. Without Try Catch, the entire batch fails. In production, every process that handles batch data should have Try Catch. In the Catch branch, you typically log the error, send a notification, and write the failed document to a dead letter queue or error folder.
process call: Process Call invokes another Boomi process as a reusable subprocess. | Capabilities: Supports modular integration design and reuse of common logic. | Interview Context: I use subprocesses for reusable functions such as validation, common authentication preparation or standardized error handling instead of duplicating logic across many processes.
process route: The Process Route Shape dynamically routes documents to independent sub-processes at runtime based on parameters, without hardcoding process dependencies. | Capabilities: Routes to sub-processes by name or ID at runtime; passes documents as input to the target process; receives return documents from the called process; allows sub-processes to be deployed and versioned independently; supports dynamic routing based on document content or properties. | Interview Context: Process Route is the decoupling champion. Instead of Process A directly calling Process B (which creates a hard dependency), Process A routes to 'whichever process handles this document type.' This means you can update Process B without redeploying Process A. In large enterprises, this is how you build integration frameworks — a main orchestration process routes to specialized handler processes. The trade-off is slightly more overhead than a direct Process Call, but the flexibility is worth it.
message shape: The Message Shape generates a new document with static or dynamic content, typically used for creating test data, notification payloads, or seed documents. | Capabilities: Creates documents from static text, XML, or JSON templates; supports dynamic content via property substitution; can generate multiple documents; commonly used with No Data start shapes for testing; useful for creating request payloads in API orchestration. | Interview Context: Message is your 'Hello World' generator. Need to test a Map shape? Use a Message shape with sample JSON. Need to send a static SOAP envelope to a web service? Message shape with the XML template. In real projects, it's often used in API orchestration — you receive a REST request, use a Message shape to construct a SOAP envelope, then call the legacy SOAP service. Simple but powerful.
notify shape: The Notify Shape sends email or SMTP-based alerts during process execution, typically used for error notifications or completion confirmations. | Capabilities: Sends emails to configurable recipients; supports dynamic subject and body content from document data; can attach documents or logs; uses SMTP connection settings; supports HTML and plain text formats; commonly used in error handling paths. | Interview Context: Notify is the 'pager' of your integration. When a process fails, the Notify shape sends an email to the ops team with the error details. In production, you typically put a Notify shape in the Catch branch of a Try Catch, and another in the Exception path. Best practice: don't send one email per failed document in a large batch — that'll flood your inbox. Instead, aggregate errors and send a summary. Better yet, integrate with a proper alerting system like PagerDuty via the HTTP Client connector.
exception shape: The Exception Shape handles process-level errors that occur outside of document-specific failures, such as connector unavailability or system timeouts. | Capabilities: Catches process-level exceptions (All Errors, Connection Errors, Shape Errors); can trigger notifications or alternative processing paths; supports custom error messages and logging; works alongside Try Catch for comprehensive error handling; can stop the process or continue with reduced functionality. | Interview Context: Exception is for 'the database is down' or 'the API returned a 503.' It's process-level, not document-level. If you have a batch of 1000 documents and the SFTP server disconnects, the Exception shape catches that. Contrast this with Try Catch, which handles 'this one document has bad data.' In production processes, you almost always have both: Try Catch for document errors, Exception for system errors.
dynamic document property: A Dynamic Document Property is document-level metadata attached directly to individual document payloads that tracks values per document throughout branching, mapping, and splitting. | Capabilities: supports per-document values that survive mapping, branching, splitting, and sub-process calls; values are set and retrieved via the Set Properties shape or scripting; each document in a batch carries its own independent value; wiped clean when the execution completes. | Interview Context: Dynamic Document Properties are the per-document counterpart to Dynamic Process Properties. If a batch contains 10,000 documents, every document carries its own Dynamic Document Property value — ideal for a source filename, a correlation ID, or a flag set earlier in the flow. They survive branching (each branch reads the document’s own value) and are often combined with the Set Properties shape to annotate a document before routing. Because they are not shared across documents and are discarded when the process finishes, they are the right choice whenever the metadata must follow the individual document rather than the whole execution.
dynamic process property: A Dynamic Process Property is a global execution variable with no predefined schema that persists throughout the entire execution lifecycle, including parent and child sub-processes. | Capabilities: Accessible across the entire execution instance; set and retrieved dynamically via scripting or the Set Properties shape; survives sub-process calls; does not maintain per-document state (shared across all documents in the execution); wiped clean when the execution completes. | Interview Context: Dynamic Process Properties are your global variables. 'Set a property called BatchID at the start of the process, and every shape downstream can read it.' They're perfect for correlation IDs, batch timestamps, or flags that need to be checked in multiple places. But remember: they're global to the execution, not per-document. If you have 10,000 documents in a batch, they all see the same Dynamic Process Property value. For per-document state, use Dynamic Document Properties instead.
process property: A Process Property is a reusable, persisted key-value container with defined data types that can maintain values across different process execution runs. | Capabilities: Can be extended via Environment Extensions; persists values across execution runs (e.g., Last Run Date, Tracking IDs); supports various data types (string, number, date, boolean); can be encrypted for sensitive values; accessible within the process and its sub-processes; configurable default values. | Interview Context: Process Properties are essential for delta loads and incremental syncs. You store the 'Last Run Date' in a Process Property, and on the next execution, you read it and query only records modified since that date. Then you update the Process Property with the current timestamp. Without this, you'd do full loads every time. Process Properties are also great for environment-specific configuration — things like API endpoint URLs or feature flags. The key difference from Dynamic Process Properties: Process Properties are defined in the component library and can be extended per environment; Dynamic Process Properties are created on-the-fly during execution.
environment extension: Environment Extension separates deployment-specific configuration from the packaged integration component. | Capabilities: Can override connection settings, operation settings, process properties, dynamic process properties, cross reference tables, trading partner settings and certificates depending on the component. | Interview Context: It is fundamental to CI/CD because the same process package can move from DEV to TEST to PROD while endpoints and credentials are supplied by the target environment.
cross reference table: A Cross Reference Table translates equivalent business values between systems. | Example: Salesforce country/state code to an ERP code, source status to target status, or partner-specific values. | Interview Answer: I use a CRT instead of hardcoding large if/else conditions inside maps. This makes business translations easier to maintain and allows values to be managed without changing the core process. | Follow-up: Explain exact matching, default behavior, environment-specific values and when to use a Business Rules shape instead.
document cache: The Document Cache is an in-memory or local-disk indexed data store that caches documents based on defined index keys, enabling ultra-fast lookups without repetitive database or HTTP calls. | Capabilities: Caches documents with configurable index keys; supports multiple cache instances per process; enables 1-to-many joins in Map shapes; persists across shape executions within a process; configurable cache size and eviction policies; supports both in-memory and disk-backed caching. | Interview Context: This is your performance savior. Without Document Cache, if you're processing 100,000 orders and each order needs to look up a customer from a database, that's 100,000 database queries — the classic N+1 problem. With Document Cache, you load all 50,000 customers into cache once (using Add to Cache), then each order does an in-memory lookup. The difference is minutes vs. hours. In interviews, always mention cache warming — loading the cache at the start of the process — and cache sizing to avoid OutOfMemory errors.
xml: XML is a hierarchical, tag-based data format commonly used for enterprise integrations and SOAP services. | Core Concepts: XML contains elements, attributes, namespaces and a root element, and its structure can be validated against schemas such as XSD. | Interview Context: In Boomi, XML is represented through XML profiles and is frequently transformed through Maps.
json: JSON is a lightweight hierarchical data format widely used by REST APIs. | Core Concepts: JSON contains objects, arrays, keys and values and can represent nested structures. | Interview Context: In Boomi, JSON is commonly represented with JSON profiles and mapped to or from XML, flat files, database structures or other JSON payloads.
xml profile: An XML Profile describes the hierarchical structure of an XML payload. | Core Elements: Root element, child elements, attributes, namespaces, data types, occurrence rules and repeating structures. | Interview Answer: I create an XML profile when Boomi needs to understand the source or target XML schema. The profile controls how the XML is parsed or generated, while the Map handles transformation. | Follow-up: Be ready for namespaces, XSDs, optional versus required elements, repeating nodes and XPath-style data selection.
json profile: A JSON Profile describes the object, array, property and data-type structure of a JSON document. | Core Elements: Objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, nulls, nested structures and occurrence rules. | Interview Answer: I use a JSON profile to make the payload strongly understood by Boomi before mapping or downstream processing. For API integrations, I commonly map between JSON profiles and another JSON, XML, database or application profile. | Follow-up: Know arrays versus objects, nested arrays, missing versus null values and how malformed JSON is handled.
flat file profile: A Flat File Profile defines the structure of delimited or fixed-width text data. | Capabilities: Specifies fields, record structure, delimiters, positions, lengths and related parsing rules. | Interview Context: I use it for CSV-like or legacy files and pay close attention to headers, trailers, delimiters, quotes and record identifiers.
identifier: An identifier is a value used to identify a record, transaction, object or segment within a data structure. | Capabilities: In integration formats it can distinguish record types, objects or business entities and is often used for routing or parsing. | Interview Context: When discussing EDI or flat files, I explain the identifier as the value that tells Boomi what type of record it is dealing with.
qualifier: A qualifier adds context to an identifier or data value by specifying what the value represents. | Capabilities: Common in EDI and hierarchical data structures where the same field position can represent different meanings based on a qualifier. | Interview Context: I explain identifier plus qualifier as 'what is this field or record?' plus 'what specifically does this value represent?' and use the combination when parsing business formats.
delimiter: A delimiter is a character that separates fields, records or segments in a structured text format. | Capabilities: Common delimiters include comma, pipe, tab and EDI separators. | Interview Context: Incorrect delimiter configuration can cause shifted fields or parsing failures, so I validate the actual source file against the profile definition.
namespace: An XML namespace distinguishes element names that might otherwise conflict and provides a namespace URI for qualification. | Capabilities: Namespace prefixes provide readable aliases for namespace URIs in XML documents. | Interview Context: Namespace mismatches are a common cause of XML mapping or XPath-style lookup issues, so I verify the namespace URI rather than relying only on the visible prefix.
rest api: REST API is an HTTP-based integration style where resources are accessed through standard HTTP methods and representations such as JSON. | Capabilities: Supports GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE patterns with headers, query parameters, path parameters and response status codes. | Interview Context: In Boomi I commonly use HTTP Client for consuming REST APIs and API Management or API Service capabilities when exposing governed APIs.
http client connector: The HTTP Client Connector is Boomi's generic REST and HTTP integration connector that enables communication with any system exposing HTTP-based APIs. | Capabilities: Supports GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, and custom HTTP methods; handles Basic Auth, OAuth 1.0/2.0, AWS Signature, API Key, and Custom Token authentication; supports multipart form uploads, file compression, and custom headers; configurable connection timeouts, read timeouts, and retry counts; supports cookie management and response code handling; new API Key authentication type configurable via encrypted Environment Extensions. | Interview Context: This is the Swiss Army knife of Boomi connectors. If a system has a REST API, HTTP Client connects to it. The Connection component holds the base URL and auth credentials; the Operation component defines the HTTP method, endpoint path, and request/response profiles. For resilience, always set connection timeouts (say, 30 seconds) and retry counts (3 retries with exponential backoff). For OAuth 2.0, Boomi handles token refresh automatically — you just configure the token endpoint, client ID, and client secret. The new API Key auth type (2026) lets you pass keys as headers, query params, or cookies via extensions.
http server: HTTP Server or listener capability allows a Boomi process to receive inbound HTTP requests. | Capabilities: Exposes an endpoint that can receive requests and pass them into the integration process. | Interview Context: I use an HTTP listener for webhook-style or real-time inbound integrations when an external system needs to call Boomi.
soap: SOAP is a protocol-based web service style that uses XML messages and commonly relies on WSDL to define service operations and data contracts. | Capabilities: Supports structured request/response messaging, headers and enterprise web-service standards. | Interview Context: I typically use SOAP when integrating with legacy or enterprise systems that expose WSDL-based services, while REST is more common for modern lightweight APIs.
oauth 2.0: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework used to obtain access tokens for protected APIs. | Capabilities: Common grant patterns include Client Credentials and Authorization Code, with refresh-token behavior depending on the provider. | Interview Context: I treat OAuth as authorization rather than simply authentication and verify the provider's exact token flow, scopes, token endpoint and refresh behavior.
jwt: JSON Web Token is a compact signed token format commonly used to carry claims between systems. | Capabilities: A JWT commonly contains header, payload and signature sections and can support stateless authorization when validated correctly. | Interview Context: I distinguish JWT from OAuth: JWT is a token format, while OAuth is an authorization framework that may issue access tokens in various formats.
api gateway: API Gateway is a centralized ingress and governance layer for APIs. | Capabilities: Depending on the Boomi API management setup, it can enforce authentication, policies, traffic controls and routing while shielding backend runtimes from direct consumer traffic. | Interview Context: I use the gateway to separate external API concerns from internal process execution and to apply consistent governance.
api management: Boomi API Management provides governance around APIs exposed by integration processes. | Core Capabilities: API publishing, policies, authentication/authorization integration, traffic controls, lifecycle management and consumer-facing API management depending on the deployed API architecture. | Interview Answer: I separate the integration implementation from API governance so consumer traffic is controlled through a managed API layer rather than exposing runtime processes directly. | Follow-up: Explain rate limiting, authentication, versioning, policies, API lifecycle and monitoring.
api key: An API key is a credential-like token used by an API provider to identify or authorize a calling application. | Capabilities: Often supplied through a header or query parameter, though header usage is generally preferable where supported. | Interview Context: I treat API keys as secrets, store them securely and do not hardcode them into process logic.
mtls: Mutual TLS is a TLS authentication pattern in which both client and server authenticate using certificates. | Capabilities: Provides encrypted transport plus client identity verification using certificates. | Interview Context: I use mTLS when a partner requires strong machine-to-machine identity rather than username/password authentication.
sftp: SFTP is the Secure File Transfer Protocol used over SSH to securely exchange files between Boomi and remote file servers. | Core Components: The Boomi SFTP connector is configured with a Connection for endpoint/authentication details and an Operation for the file action. | Authentication: Common configurations include username/password and key-based SSH authentication. | Operations: The current SFTP connector supports inbound Read, List and Listen, and outbound Write and Delete. | Capabilities: Supports remote directories, file filtering, post-read actions such as move/delete/rename, listing, sorting and file metadata. | Interview Context: A common pattern is to poll an SFTP folder, process each file, transform the contents, send the result downstream and then archive or move the successful file while routing failures for investigation.
sftp connection: The SFTP Connection contains the server-level configuration used to establish an SFTP session. | Core Settings: Host, port, username, authentication method, password or SSH key information, remote directory and other transport settings depending on the connector version. | Interview Context: I keep endpoint and credentials in the Connection and avoid putting environment-specific values directly into process logic; those settings can be exposed through Environment Extensions.
sftp operation: The SFTP Operation defines what action Boomi performs against an SFTP server and the file/object structure involved. | Operations: Current SFTP supports Read, List, Listen, Write and Delete. | Interview Context: I create separate operations for the distinct file actions my integration needs and choose the operation based on whether I am ingesting, listing, monitoring, creating or deleting files.
sftp read: SFTP Read is an inbound operation that retrieves the content of a specific file from an SFTP server. | Capabilities: The file name is used to identify the file, and remote directory information can be supplied through configured or dynamic properties as supported. | Interview Context: I use Read when the process already knows which file to retrieve, and I pay attention to action-after-read behavior to prevent duplicate processing.
sftp write: SFTP Write is an outbound operation used to upload or create files on a remote SFTP server. | Capabilities: Supports file naming, remote directory targeting, batch-oriented transfer and configurable behavior when a file already exists. | Interview Context: I use Write when sending generated files to a partner and explicitly decide what should happen if the destination file already exists.
sftp list: SFTP List retrieves metadata for files in a remote directory based on configured criteria. | Capabilities: Can return one JSON document per listed file, supports filtering and can optionally perform post-actions such as move or delete for file objects. | Interview Context: I use List when I need to discover available files first and then control which files should be processed.
sftp listen: SFTP Listen monitors a remote directory for supported file events such as creation, modification or deletion. | Capabilities: It can trigger integration processing from file events instead of relying only on scheduled polling. | Interview Context: I use Listen when near-real-time file arrival processing is required and the runtime/cloud attachment supports the listener model.
sftp authentication: SFTP authentication establishes the identity of the client connecting to the SSH-based file server. | Common Methods: Username/password and public/private-key based authentication are common; exact options depend on the current connector configuration and partner requirements. | Interview Context: For production partner integrations I prefer key-based authentication when required by the partner, protect private keys and validate host/server trust requirements.
sftp duplicate file: Duplicate file handling is the design used to prevent the same SFTP file from being processed more than once. | Techniques: Use controlled post-read actions such as move or archive, unique naming conventions, business identifiers, tracking and idempotent downstream processing. | Interview Context: I never assume a file listener or scheduler alone guarantees business-level exactly-once processing; I design explicit duplicate protection.
database connector: The Database Connector is Boomi's relational database integration interface that enables SQL-based data operations using JDBC drivers. | Capabilities: Dynamic SQL queries, stored procedure calls, and batch inserts/upserts; supports connection pooling and distributed transactions; configurable batch counts for optimized commit intervals; supports all major databases (Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL, DB2, Snowflake); improved SQL parsing for objects and columns containing spaces (2026); optimized performance for large record sets (>1000 records). | Interview Context: The Database Connector is your direct line to relational data. For bulk loads, set batch counts between 500-1000 records per commit — this balances throughput with transaction safety. For updates, use UPSERT operations to handle both inserts and updates in one pass. Connection pooling is critical — configure min/max pool sizes based on your Flow Control thread count. If you have 10 threads, you need at least 10 connections in the pool. One pro tip: for delta loads, always use a Process Property to store the Last Run Date, then query WHERE ModifiedDate > ? with that property value.
jdbc: JDBC is the Java Database Connectivity standard used to connect Java applications to relational databases. | Capabilities: Provides drivers and APIs for executing SQL and database operations. | Interview Context: In Boomi, the Database Connector relies on JDBC drivers to communicate with supported databases, so driver compatibility and connection settings matter in runtime deployments.
stored procedure: A stored procedure is a database-side program that encapsulates SQL and business logic. | Capabilities: Boomi can invoke stored procedures through database operations where supported, passing inputs and receiving outputs or result sets. | Interview Context: I use stored procedures when the database owns complex transactional logic, but I avoid moving integration orchestration into the database unnecessarily.
upsert: Upsert means inserting a record when it does not exist and updating it when it already exists. | Capabilities: Reduces separate existence-check logic and is common in synchronization integrations. | Interview Context: I use upsert for master-data synchronization when the target supports a reliable business key, while ensuring the operation is idempotent and the key is properly indexed.
delta load: Delta load transfers only records that changed since the previous successful processing point. | Capabilities: Reduces volume and processing time compared with full loads and commonly uses timestamps, sequence numbers or change tracking. | Interview Context: I usually store a reliable watermark such as last successful modified timestamp and update it only after the corresponding batch is successfully processed.
full load: Full load transfers the complete source dataset rather than only changes. | Capabilities: Useful for initial migration, reconciliation or systems where incremental change tracking is unavailable. | Interview Context: For large datasets I assess whether a full load can fit within runtime, database and API limits and often combine it with batching and restartability.
edi: EDI is Electronic Data Interchange, a standardized way for businesses to exchange structured business documents electronically. | Capabilities: Common standards include ANSI X12 and EDIFACT, with transactions such as purchase orders, invoices and shipping notices. | Interview Context: In Boomi, EDI work often combines profiles, trading partners, validation, transformation, acknowledgements and secure B2B transport.
x12: X12 is a common EDI standard used to exchange structured business documents between trading partners. | Core Structure: ISA is the interchange envelope, GS is the functional-group envelope, ST starts a transaction set, and corresponding trailer segments close those levels. | Interview Answer: In Boomi, I typically receive an X12 document, use an EDI/X12 profile to parse it, validate the structure, map business data into the target system format, and generate the required response such as an acknowledgment when applicable. | Follow-up: Know ISA/IEA, GS/GE, ST/SE, transaction-set IDs, sender/receiver IDs, qualifiers, control numbers and acknowledgments.
trading partner: A Trading Partner in Boomi is a B2B configuration entity that defines the communication protocols, security settings, and document standards for exchanging data with external business partners. | Capabilities: Configures AS2, SFTP, FTPS, and HTTP communication methods; manages partner-specific certificates and encryption keys; defines EDI standards (X12, EDIFACT, HL7) and document types; supports partner-specific envelopes and control numbers; maintains partner profiles independently from integration processes; new unified SFTP communication method with full connector capabilities (2026). | Interview Context: Trading Partners are the heart of B2B integration. Instead of hardcoding partner details in every process, you create a Trading Partner profile once and reference it everywhere. The profile has the partner's AS2 ID, SFTP credentials, EDI identifiers (ISA/GS control numbers for X12), and certificates. When a new trading partner is onboarded, you just create a new profile — no process changes needed. The 2026 update unified the SFTP communication method, so Trading Partner SFTP now has the same capabilities as the standalone SFTP connector. This eliminates the old workaround of using separate connectors for B2B file transfers.
edi envelope: An EDI envelope wraps business transactions with control information needed to identify senders, receivers and transaction boundaries. | X12 Structure: Common envelope levels are ISA/IEA, GS/GE and ST/SE. | Interview Context: Envelope errors can prevent an EDI document from being accepted even when the business transaction itself is correct, so I validate identifiers, control numbers and delimiters.
qualifier in edi: An EDI qualifier provides context for an identifier, such as defining what a particular partner or location code represents. | Capabilities: Qualifiers allow standardized identifiers to carry precise semantic meaning within EDI segments. | Interview Context: When troubleshooting EDI, I verify both the identifier and qualifier because changing either can change the business interpretation of the record.
synchronous: Synchronous integration means the caller waits for a response before completing the interaction. | Characteristics: Request and response are coupled in time, so latency and downstream availability directly affect the caller. | Interview Context: I choose synchronous processing for real-time APIs where the caller needs an immediate result, but I avoid it for long-running workloads where asynchronous processing is more resilient.
asynchronous: Asynchronous integration separates the producer from the consumer in time so the producer does not need to wait for downstream processing to finish. | Capabilities: Queues, events and scheduled workers can provide buffering and resilience. | Interview Context: I prefer asynchronous architecture for high-volume or long-running workloads where decoupling, retry and spike absorption are more important than immediate response.
coupled: Coupled integration has a strong dependency between communicating systems, often in timing, availability or interface structure. | Risk: A failure or change in one system can directly affect the other. | Interview Context: Point-to-point synchronous calls are often tightly coupled, so I look for queues, APIs, canonical models or reusable services when decoupling is valuable.
decoupled: Decoupled integration reduces direct dependency between producer and consumer systems. | Capabilities: Messaging, queues, events, APIs and independent processes can isolate failures and allow systems to evolve separately. | Interview Context: For high-volume integrations I often use asynchronous queues or event-driven patterns so downstream outages do not immediately block the producer.
point to point: Point-to-point integration directly connects one source system to one target system. | Benefit: Simple for a small number of integrations. | Risk: Complexity grows rapidly as the number of systems and connections increases. | Interview Context: I use point-to-point for genuinely simple integrations, but at enterprise scale I prefer reusable APIs, eventing or centralized integration patterns.
event driven architecture: Event-driven architecture uses events to notify interested consumers that something happened. | Capabilities: Producers publish events without requiring every consumer to be called synchronously, enabling loose coupling and independent scaling. | Interview Context: I use event-driven architecture when business events such as order-created or customer-updated need multiple downstream consumers or near-real-time processing.
publish subscribe: Publish/Subscribe is a messaging pattern in which a producer publishes a message or event to a topic and multiple subscribers can independently consume it. | Benefit: Producers do not need direct knowledge of every consumer. | Interview Context: Pub/Sub is useful when the same business event must feed several downstream integrations without creating separate synchronous calls.
queue: A queue buffers messages between producers and consumers. | Capabilities: Supports asynchronous processing, workload smoothing, retry patterns and consumer scaling depending on the technology. | Interview Context: I use a queue when I need to absorb traffic spikes or isolate a downstream system from the producer's timing.
api: An API is a defined interface through which software systems communicate. | Capabilities: APIs can expose operations, resources, events or data through contracts such as REST, SOAP or other protocols. | Interview Context: I treat an API as a contract, not merely a URL, and consider authentication, versioning, error responses, idempotency and observability as part of the design.
idempotency: Idempotency means processing the same business request more than once does not create an unintended duplicate business result. | Common Technique: Store a unique business key or event ID and check whether it has already been processed before committing the transaction. | Interview Answer: I design idempotency whenever retries or duplicate messages are possible. For example, before creating a customer or order, I validate a unique source-system ID against the target or an idempotency store. | Follow-up: Explain why retries can create duplicates and where the idempotency key should be stored.
retry: Retry is a resilience mechanism that attempts a failed operation again when the failure may be temporary. | Best Use: Network timeouts, transient HTTP 5xx responses, temporary database unavailability or throttling. | Interview Answer: I distinguish transient failures from permanent business or validation failures. I use controlled retries with appropriate backoff and a maximum attempt count, then route persistent failures to an error or DLQ path. | Follow-up: Explain exponential backoff, retry storms, idempotency and when not to retry.
dead letter queue: A Dead Letter Queue is a controlled holding area for messages that repeatedly fail processing. | Core Purpose: Prevent poison messages from blocking the normal flow while preserving the failed payload and context for investigation or replay. | Interview Answer: I route unrecoverable or repeatedly failed messages to a DLQ with correlation information, error details and source metadata. Support can then correct the root cause and replay the message safely. | Follow-up: Explain retry count, poison messages, alerting, replay safety and idempotency.
rate limiting: Rate limiting restricts the number of requests sent or accepted during a defined period. | Purpose: Protects APIs and downstream systems from overload and enforces provider quotas. | Interview Context: I consider vendor API limits when choosing Flow Control, batching, queueing and retry strategies.
throttling: Throttling deliberately slows or limits processing concurrency or request rate. | Purpose: Protects downstream systems and runtime resources while maintaining predictable throughput. | Interview Context: If a target API supports only a certain request rate, I throttle Boomi rather than maximizing concurrency blindly.
cicd: CI/CD is the automated practice of validating, packaging and deploying software changes through controlled environments. | Boomi Context: Platform APIs and DevOps tooling can automate packaging, deployment and environment-specific configuration. | Interview Context: A mature Boomi CI/CD pipeline moves versioned components through DEV, TEST/UAT and PROD with automated checks and externalized configuration.
deployment: Deployment in Boomi is the act of promoting a packaged integration from one environment to another — for example, from TEST to PROD. | Capabilities: Supports both manual UI-based deployments and automated deployments via AtomSphere API; validates component compatibility before deployment; applies environment extensions during deployment; maintains deployment audit trail; supports scheduled deployments and deployment windows. | Interview Context: Deployment is more than just copying files. Boomi validates that all dependencies are present, applies the target environment's extensions, and updates the runtime's component cache. For production deployments, you should always use the AtomSphere API within your CI/CD pipeline — Jenkins, GitLab, Azure DevOps — rather than manual UI clicks. This eliminates human error and provides an audit trail that compliance teams love.
environment: An Environment in Boomi is a logical deployment boundary that represents a stage in your software development lifecycle — typically DEV, TEST, and PROD. | Capabilities: Isolates runtime configurations, credentials, and endpoints per stage; supports environment-specific extensions that override process properties and connection settings; enables controlled promotion of packages from lower to higher environments; maintains separate execution history and logs per environment. | Interview Context: Environments are the foundation of Boomi CI/CD. You build in DEV, package it, deploy to TEST for QA validation, then promote to PROD. Each environment has its own Atom/Molecule attached. The key insight: a single process can be deployed to multiple environments, but each environment can have completely different connection strings, credentials, and property values via Environment Extensions. This means zero code changes between environments.
environment group: An Environment Group organizes environments and can simplify deployment and runtime management in larger accounts. | Capabilities: Provides logical grouping for lifecycle and operational administration. | Interview Context: I use environment organization to make promotion paths and production boundaries clear.
process property component: A Process Property component is a reusable property definition that can hold values used by processes. | Capabilities: Properties can be exposed through environment extensions for deployment-specific values. | Interview Context: I use it for configuration that belongs to the integration design but should not be hardcoded, such as business thresholds or endpoint-related parameters.
platform api: Boomi Platform API provides programmatic access to platform management functions. | Capabilities: It can support automation around components, deployments, environments, monitoring and other platform operations depending on the API surface and account permissions. | Interview Context: I use platform APIs when an enterprise needs automated CI/CD, governance, reporting or operational tooling instead of manual UI-only administration.
monitoring: Boomi monitoring is the operational practice of observing process executions, logs, documents, runtimes and failures. | Capabilities: Process reporting and logs help identify execution status, errors, timing and runtime behavior. | Interview Context: In production support I correlate execution time, process, runtime, document identifiers and downstream error details before deciding on recovery.
root cause analysis: Root Cause Analysis identifies the underlying reason for an integration failure rather than treating only the visible error. | Method: Correlate timestamp, execution, document, connector, runtime, downstream response and recent deployment/configuration changes. | Interview Context: I avoid simply rerunning failed processes; I first establish whether the cause is data, configuration, authentication, connectivity, capacity or a downstream system issue.
authentication: Authentication verifies who or what is connecting to a system. | Examples: Username/password, API key, OAuth token, certificate, SSH key and mutual TLS. | Interview Context: I distinguish authentication from authorization and choose the method required by the partner or API provider.
authorization: Authorization determines what an authenticated identity is allowed to access or perform. | Examples: OAuth scopes, roles, permissions and API policies. | Interview Context: A valid token proves identity or delegated access, but the token still needs the correct scopes or permissions for the requested operation.
ssl tls: TLS provides encrypted communication and server or client identity validation for network connections. | Capabilities: HTTPS, secure database connections and other protocols can rely on TLS. | Interview Context: When troubleshooting secure connectivity I verify certificate chain, hostname, truststore/keystore requirements, protocol compatibility and expiration.
certificate: A digital certificate binds an identity to a public key and is used in TLS, signing or authentication scenarios. | Capabilities: Boomi integrations may use certificates for HTTPS, mTLS, partner security and other secure protocols. | Interview Context: Certificate troubleshooting includes checking expiration, chain, trust and whether the correct certificate is deployed to the target runtime.
transaction: A transaction is a logical unit of work that should satisfy defined consistency and commit rules. | Integration Context: Database transactions can control groups of database operations, while distributed integration steps often require explicit compensation or idempotency rather than assuming a single atomic transaction. | Interview Context: I never assume an end-to-end Boomi process is one atomic transaction across unrelated systems.
batch processing: Batch processing handles a group of records or files together rather than waiting for one real-time request at a time. | Capabilities: Useful for scheduled files, bulk database loads and large data synchronization. | Interview Context: I optimize batch integrations around document count, batch size, memory, database commits and restartability.
real time integration: Real-time integration processes data immediately or with very low latency after an event or request. | Capabilities: APIs, listeners and event-driven triggers can support real-time or near-real-time patterns. | Interview Context: Real-time does not automatically mean synchronous; an event can trigger asynchronous processing while still providing near-immediate ingestion.
near real time: Near-real-time integration processes changes with a small delay rather than requiring an immediate synchronous response. | Examples: Polling every minute, event queues or listener-based processing. | Interview Context: I use near-real-time when the business needs fast updates but can tolerate seconds or minutes of delay.
agile: Agile is an iterative software delivery approach that emphasizes incremental delivery, feedback and adaptation. | Capabilities: Common practices include backlog refinement, sprint planning, daily collaboration, reviews and retrospectives. | Interview Context: As an integration lead I connect Agile delivery to integration dependencies, testing, environment promotion and production readiness.
sdLC: SDLC is the Software Development Life Cycle covering activities from requirements through design, development, testing, deployment and maintenance. | Integration Context: A Boomi change typically moves through design, development, peer review, testing, UAT, release and production monitoring. | Interview Context: I explain SDLC in terms of controlled delivery rather than only coding.
50k transactions per hour: A 50,000-transactions-per-hour requirement is primarily a capacity, concurrency and resilience architecture problem. | Design Approach: Evaluate runtime cluster capacity, process parallelism, connector connection pools, downstream API/database limits, batching, queueing and monitoring. | Interview Context: I would not simply increase Flow Control; I would calculate throughput per worker, identify the bottleneck and decouple the workload with queues when downstream systems cannot absorb peak traffic.
100k records: Processing 100,000 records requires explicit attention to memory, batching, concurrency, restartability and downstream limits. | Design Approach: Stream or batch where appropriate, avoid loading unnecessary reference data repeatedly, use Document Cache for reusable lookup data and design checkpoint/restart behavior. | Interview Context: I first identify whether the 100,000 records arrive as one file, many documents or API pages because the optimal design changes with the input model.
database unavailable: When a database is unavailable, the integration should fail predictably rather than creating uncontrolled retries or data loss. | Response: Apply bounded retry for transient connectivity, capture failed documents, alert operations and use queueing or replay where appropriate. | Interview Context: I distinguish temporary database outage from invalid SQL or authentication failure and avoid retrying permanent errors indefinitely.
api timeout: An API timeout means Boomi did not receive a response within the configured time, but it does not necessarily prove the target did not process the request. | Risk: Blind retry can create duplicates if the original request succeeded. | Interview Context: I use idempotency keys or business identifiers where possible and design retry behavior based on the API's semantics.
runtime node failure: A runtime node failure is handled differently depending on whether the workload is deployed to a single runtime or a runtime cluster. | Design: A cluster provides additional nodes and can improve availability, while process state and external dependencies still need to be resilient. | Interview Context: I test failure scenarios rather than assuming clustering alone guarantees zero downtime.
large file: Large-file processing can create memory and throughput pressure if the entire payload is repeatedly materialized or transformed inefficiently. | Approach: Use appropriate file handling, minimize unnecessary copies, process in manageable units where possible and monitor heap and runtime resources. | Interview Context: I first determine file size, format, transformation complexity and downstream requirements before choosing the processing strategy.
production incident: A production integration incident is an operational event that affects data flow, business processing or service availability. | Response: Stabilize first, identify impact, preserve evidence, isolate the failing component, recover safely, communicate status and complete RCA afterward. | Interview Context: As a lead, I focus on business impact and safe recovery first, then permanent corrective action.
zero downtime integration: Zero-downtime integration is an availability goal where releases or infrastructure failures should not interrupt required business processing. | Architecture: Requires redundant runtime capacity, controlled deployment, resilient dependencies and careful release/rollback procedures. | Interview Context: I would never promise zero downtime from a single Boomi setting; it is an end-to-end architecture and operational discipline.
ddp vs dpp: Dynamic Document Property is scoped to an individual document, while Dynamic Process Property is scoped to the process execution. | DDP: Best for document-specific metadata such as file name, correlation ID or routing key. | DPP: Best for execution-level shared state or control values. | Interview Context: The deciding question is 'does this value belong to this document or to this execution?'
process property vs environment extensio: A Process Property defines reusable integration configuration, while an Environment Extension supplies or overrides values for a specific deployment environment. | Process Property: Defines the property in the integration design. | Environment Extension: Keeps DEV/TEST/PROD values outside the packaged logic. | Interview Context: I use both together so the process remains reusable while each environment provides its own value.
atom vs runtime: Atom is the legacy name for a basic single-node Boomi runtime. | Current Terminology: Boomi now prefers Runtime and Basic Runtime terminology after its 2025 terminology update. | Interview Context: I recognize Atom in older documentation and interviews but use Runtime when discussing the current platform.
molecule vs runtime cluster: Molecule is the legacy name for a clustered single-tenant runtime, while Runtime Cluster is the current terminology. | Capabilities: Both describe multi-node runtime architecture intended to increase capacity and availability. | Interview Context: If an interviewer says Molecule, I answer using the familiar term and then clarify the current Runtime Cluster terminology.
sftp vs ftp: SFTP transfers files through SSH and provides secure encrypted transport, while traditional FTP is a separate protocol and does not provide the same built-in encryption. | Interview Context: For production partner file exchange I normally prefer SFTP when the partner supports it because credentials and file data are protected in transit.
rest vs soap: REST is an architectural style commonly implemented over HTTP with lightweight representations such as JSON, while SOAP is a protocol-based XML web-service standard commonly described by WSDL. | Interview Context: I choose based on the provider contract and enterprise requirements rather than assuming REST is always better.
synchronous vs asynchronous: Synchronous processing keeps the caller waiting for the response, while asynchronous processing allows work to continue independently. | Interview Context: I use synchronous patterns for immediate request/response use cases and asynchronous patterns for high-volume, long-running or decoupled workloads.
batch vs real time: Batch processes groups of records at scheduled or controlled intervals, while real-time processing reacts to requests or events with low latency. | Interview Context: The decision depends on business latency requirements, source capabilities, target capacity and operational complexity.
connection vs operation: Connection defines how and where to connect; Operation defines what action to perform and what data structure is involved. | Interview Context: This separation allows the same endpoint configuration to be reused across multiple actions and makes environment-specific endpoint credentials easier to externalize.
map vs data process: Map primarily transforms a document from one profile structure to another, while Data Process is used for broader document manipulation tasks such as splitting, combining or other configured processing. | Interview Context: If the requirement is source-to-target field transformation I start with Map; if it is document manipulation I consider Data Process.
queue vs pub sub: A queue typically distributes a message to one consumer or consumer group, while Publish/Subscribe allows multiple subscribers to independently receive an event. | Interview Context: I use queues for work distribution and buffering, and Pub/Sub when the same event needs to fan out to multiple independent consumers.
authentication vs authorization: Authentication answers 'who are you?' while authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?'. | Interview Context: In API troubleshooting I check both: a valid identity/token may still fail if it lacks the required role or scope.
retry vs replay: Retry repeats a failed operation as part of the active processing flow, while replay generally means intentionally reprocessing a previously captured failed message or document. | Interview Context: Retry should be bounded and safe; replay should be controlled and usually requires idempotency or duplicate protection.
high availability vs scalability: High Availability focuses on remaining available during failures, while scalability focuses on handling increased workload by adding or increasing capacity. | Interview Context: A runtime cluster can contribute to both, but HA and scalability are different architectural goals and should be designed and tested separately.
what is boomi: Boomi is an iPaaS platform used to connect applications, APIs, databases, files and events across cloud and on-premises systems. | Natural Answer: 'I use Boomi as the integration layer between systems. It gives us reusable connectors, transformation, orchestration, runtime management and monitoring, so instead of building point-to-point integration infrastructure ourselves, we focus mainly on the business integration logic.'
what is an atom: Atom is the legacy Boomi term for a single-node, single-tenant runtime. | Natural Answer: 'An Atom is basically a single Boomi runtime node where the deployed processes execute. It is suitable for simpler workloads, while for high availability or higher volume I would consider a Runtime Cluster, which was historically called a Molecule.'
what is a molecule: Molecule is the legacy Boomi term for a clustered single-tenant runtime. | Natural Answer: 'A Molecule is a group of runtime nodes working as one logical runtime. The main reason to use it is to distribute processing and improve availability compared with a single Atom. In current Boomi terminology this is generally referred to as a Runtime Cluster.'
what is a dynamic document property: A Dynamic Document Property stores metadata associated with an individual document. | Natural Answer: 'I use a Dynamic Document Property when the value belongs to a particular document, for example a source file name, correlation ID or routing value. The key point is that it is document-level state, unlike a Dynamic Process Property, which is execution-level state.'
what is flow control: Flow Control controls how Boomi processes documents concurrently or sequentially. | Natural Answer: 'I mainly use Flow Control to control concurrency. If I need higher throughput and the target supports parallel requests, I can process documents in parallel. If ordering or shared-state constraints matter, I use sequential processing. I always check downstream connection and API limits before increasing concurrency.'
how do you handle errors in boomi: Boomi error handling combines connector error behavior, Try/Catch, explicit exceptions, retries, notifications, logging and operational reprocessing. | Natural Answer: 'I first separate transient technical failures from permanent business or data errors. For transient issues I use bounded retry, while bad documents go through controlled error handling such as Try/Catch. I capture the document and correlation information, alert operations when required and make the recovery path idempotent so reprocessing is safe.'
how do you design high availability: High availability requires redundant runtime capacity and resilient integration dependencies rather than one configuration switch. | Natural Answer: 'For a mission-critical integration, I would use a Runtime Cluster with multiple nodes, make sure the deployment and downstream dependencies are resilient, and design retries and idempotency carefully. I would also test node failure and recovery instead of assuming the architecture is highly available just because it is clustered.'
account: An Account in Boomi is the top-level tenant or workspace that contains all your integration assets, users, environments, and runtime configurations. | Capabilities: Isolates all components, data, and execution history from other accounts; configurable user roles and permissions; supports multiple environments within one account; can be linked to SSO providers for enterprise authentication; provides usage metering and billing aggregation. | Interview Context: Your Boomi Account is your kingdom. Everything lives inside it — processes, connectors, Atoms, users. Large enterprises often have multiple accounts: one for the integration COE, one for the HR team, one for finance. Each account is completely isolated. When discussing architecture, mention that account boundaries are hard — you can't easily share components across accounts without using the Boomi Marketplace or manual XML exports.
user: A Boomi user is an identity that accesses the platform according to assigned roles and permissions. | Capabilities: Supports administration, development, monitoring and deployment access based on security configuration. | Interview Context: I follow least privilege and separate development, deployment and production-support access where required.
role: A role is a collection of platform permissions assigned to users or groups. | Capabilities: Controls which platform functions a user can perform. | Interview Context: I use role-based access rather than giving every developer unrestricted production privileges.
permission: A permission determines whether an identity can perform a particular platform action. | Capabilities: Supports controlled access to development, deployment, administration and monitoring functions. | Interview Context: Permission design is part of governance and should follow least privilege.
component explorer: Component Explorer is the platform area used to locate, organize and manage Boomi components. | Capabilities: Helps developers find reusable processes, maps, profiles, connections, operations and other assets. | Interview Context: Reuse starts with finding existing components before creating duplicates.
component version: A component version represents a saved version of a Boomi component. | Capabilities: Provides traceability and supports controlled lifecycle management. | Interview Context: I use versioning to understand exactly which component revision was tested and deployed.
component dependency: A component dependency is a reference from one Boomi component to another component it uses. | Capabilities: Dependencies can include maps, profiles, subprocesses, connections and operations. | Interview Context: Before deployment I check dependencies so a package does not fail because a referenced component is missing or incompatible.
shared component: A shared component is a reusable asset referenced by multiple processes or components. | Capabilities: Reduces duplicate configuration and centralizes common logic. | Interview Context: Shared components improve maintainability, but I assess change impact carefully because one modification can affect several integrations.
reusable component: A reusable component is an integration asset designed to be referenced by multiple processes. | Capabilities: Encourages modularity and avoids duplicated logic. | Interview Context: I commonly make validation, common transformations and utility subprocesses reusable when the behavior is genuinely shared.
packaged component: A packaged component is a prepared version of a Boomi component intended for deployment or distribution. | Capabilities: Supports controlled movement of tested assets between environments. | Interview Context: Packaging separates development activity from controlled deployment.
release: A release is a controlled delivery of a component or set of changes into a target environment. | Capabilities: Provides lifecycle traceability and deployment governance. | Interview Context: I associate a release with testing evidence, deployment scope, configuration and rollback planning.
build: Build is the design-time validation and preparation activity before a component is packaged or deployed. | Capabilities: Helps identify configuration or dependency problems before release. | Interview Context: I distinguish building a component from deploying it to a runtime.
