promote: Promotion means moving a tested component through the environment lifecycle, such as DEV to TEST or TEST to PROD. | Capabilities: Supports controlled lifecycle progression. | Interview Context: I promote the same tested logic while keeping environment-specific configuration externalized.
import: Import brings Boomi component or configuration content into an account or environment according to the supported import mechanism. | Capabilities: Useful for migration, reuse and controlled asset movement. | Interview Context: I validate imported dependencies and environment-specific configuration before execution.
export: Export packages or extracts Boomi component information for movement, backup or external lifecycle management. | Capabilities: Supports migration and component portability according to supported export formats. | Interview Context: I use controlled exports as part of migration or backup workflows, while recognizing that secrets and environment configuration require separate handling.
runtime cloud: Runtime Cloud is current terminology for Boomi-managed cloud execution infrastructure. | Capabilities: Provides managed runtime capacity without requiring the customer to install and maintain each runtime node. | Interview Context: I consider managed cloud runtime when the integration does not require customer-controlled network placement or infrastructure management.
cloud runtime: A Cloud Runtime is a Boomi-hosted execution environment for integration processes. | Capabilities: Reduces customer infrastructure administration and supports cloud-based integration execution. | Interview Context: I select cloud execution when connectivity, security and workload requirements are compatible with a managed runtime.
private cloud: Private cloud is infrastructure dedicated to a customer or controlled organization rather than shared public infrastructure. | Integration Context: A customer-managed Boomi runtime can be placed in private cloud infrastructure when internal network access or governance requires it. | Interview Context: I use private cloud for integrations that need controlled network placement but still benefit from cloud infrastructure.
hybrid integration: Hybrid integration connects cloud applications with on-premises or private systems. | Capabilities: Requires secure network connectivity and an appropriately placed runtime. | Interview Context: A common enterprise pattern is SaaS-to-on-prem integration where the runtime sits close to the internal systems while Boomi provides centralized design and management.
on premises runtime: An on-premises runtime executes Boomi integrations within customer-controlled infrastructure. | Capabilities: Provides direct access to internal databases, file servers and private applications without exposing them publicly. | Interview Context: I choose it when network or security requirements make direct internal connectivity important.
public cloud: Public cloud provides infrastructure and services hosted by a cloud provider and shared across customers through logical isolation. | Integration Context: Boomi runtimes or supporting systems can run in public cloud environments such as AWS or Azure. | Interview Context: I evaluate network connectivity, security, availability and cost rather than choosing cloud solely for convenience.
listener: A listener waits for an inbound event or request and starts or continues integration processing when the event arrives. | Capabilities: Common listener patterns include HTTP, web services, file and event-driven triggers. | Interview Context: I use listeners when the source system pushes data rather than expecting Boomi to poll on a schedule.
schedule: A schedule triggers a Boomi process at configured time intervals or calendar times. | Capabilities: Useful for polling, batch jobs, reconciliation and periodic synchronization. | Interview Context: I choose schedules when the source cannot push events or when the business process is inherently periodic.
polling: Polling repeatedly checks a source system for new or changed data. | Capabilities: Common with SFTP folders, databases and APIs that do not provide events. | Interview Context: Polling is simple but must be designed to avoid duplicate reads, excessive calls and race conditions.
webhook: A webhook is an HTTP callback where a source system sends an event or notification to a configured endpoint. | Capabilities: Provides near-real-time push behavior without continuous polling. | Interview Context: I prefer webhooks when the provider supports reliable delivery, authentication and retry semantics.
event: An event is a notification that something happened, such as an order being created or a customer being updated. | Capabilities: Events can trigger asynchronous downstream processing and multiple consumers. | Interview Context: I use events when consumers care about changes rather than requesting the entire state synchronously.
event streams: Event Streams is an event-oriented capability for moving messages or events between producers and consumers. | Capabilities: Supports asynchronous, decoupled integration patterns and can buffer workloads. | Interview Context: I consider event streaming when throughput, loose coupling and near-real-time processing are more important than synchronous request/response.
message broker: A message broker receives, stores, routes and delivers messages between producers and consumers. | Capabilities: Provides buffering, decoupling, retry and delivery control depending on the technology. | Interview Context: I use brokers to isolate systems and absorb workload spikes.
producer: A producer is the system or application that creates and publishes a message or event. | Capabilities: It can send work to a queue or publish an event without directly implementing consumer processing. | Interview Context: Decoupling producers from consumers reduces dependency on downstream timing.
consumer: A consumer is the application or process that receives and processes a message or event. | Capabilities: Consumers can scale independently depending on the messaging platform. | Interview Context: I design consumers to be idempotent because message delivery can involve retries or duplicates.
topic: A topic is a logical channel used by publish/subscribe messaging systems. | Capabilities: Multiple subscribers can consume events from the same topic independently. | Interview Context: I use topics for fan-out scenarios where several downstream applications need the same event.
acknowledgement: An acknowledgement indicates that a message or transaction was accepted or processed according to a particular protocol. | Capabilities: Can be technical, application-level or EDI-specific. | Interview Context: I distinguish transport acknowledgement from business acknowledgement because receiving a message does not always mean business processing succeeded.
poison message: A poison message is a message that repeatedly fails processing because its content or required condition cannot be successfully handled. | Capabilities: DLQs and bounded retry prevent one bad message from blocking healthy work. | Interview Context: I isolate poison messages, preserve them for investigation and avoid infinite retry loops.
backpressure: Backpressure is a mechanism or design principle that prevents a fast producer from overwhelming a slower consumer. | Capabilities: Queues, throttling, bounded concurrency and rate limits can provide backpressure. | Interview Context: I use backpressure when upstream traffic can exceed downstream processing capacity.
throughput: Throughput is the amount of data or number of transactions successfully processed per unit of time. | Capabilities: Measured in records/sec, transactions/hour, files/hour or similar units. | Interview Context: I optimize throughput only after identifying the bottleneck, because increasing Boomi concurrency cannot fix a downstream API limit.
latency: Latency is the elapsed time between an integration request/event and the resulting response or processing completion. | Capabilities: Important for synchronous and real-time integrations. | Interview Context: I distinguish latency from throughput: a system can have high throughput while individual transactions still have high latency.
concurrency: Concurrency is the number of tasks or documents being processed at the same time. | Capabilities: Higher concurrency can increase throughput but also increases CPU, memory and downstream connection usage. | Interview Context: I tune concurrency against the weakest dependency rather than maximizing it blindly.
thread: A thread is a unit of execution within the JVM. | Capabilities: Boomi runtime work can consume threads for concurrent processing and connector operations. | Interview Context: Thread starvation can occur when too many tasks block on slow dependencies, so concurrency and timeout settings must be considered together.
thread starvation: Thread starvation occurs when available execution threads are occupied or blocked so other work cannot progress efficiently. | Causes: Excessive concurrency, slow downstream calls, blocking operations or resource contention. | Interview Context: I look at execution duration, concurrency, connector latency and runtime resource usage when diagnosing it.
connection pool: A connection pool maintains reusable connections to a target system so processes do not create a new connection for every operation. | Benefits: Reduces connection setup overhead and improves throughput. | Interview Context: An oversized pool can overwhelm the database or API, so pool sizing must match downstream capacity.
timeout: A timeout defines how long an operation waits before treating a response or connection attempt as unsuccessful. | Capabilities: Protects runtime resources from indefinitely blocked calls. | Interview Context: I tune timeouts according to the downstream SLA and combine them with bounded retry and idempotency.
pagination: Pagination divides a large API result set into manageable pages. | Capabilities: Supports page number, offset, cursor or token-based retrieval depending on the API. | Interview Context: I prefer cursor or provider-recommended pagination for large datasets and design restartability around the last successfully processed page.
cursor pagination: Cursor pagination uses a provider-issued cursor or continuation token to retrieve the next page of data. | Benefit: Usually more stable than offset pagination when records change during extraction. | Interview Context: I follow the API provider's cursor semantics and persist the continuation state carefully when restartability matters.
offset pagination: Offset pagination retrieves records using an offset and page size. | Risk: Records changing during extraction can cause skips or duplicates depending on the API behavior. | Interview Context: I use it when the provider supports it reliably, but I assess consistency for large or frequently changing datasets.
rate limit response 429: HTTP 429 indicates that a service is refusing requests because the caller has exceeded a configured request rate. | Response: Respect Retry-After where provided, throttle requests and use bounded backoff. | Interview Context: I treat 429 as a capacity/governance signal rather than an application-data error.
http status 400: HTTP 400 indicates that the server considers the request invalid. | Common Causes: Malformed JSON, missing fields, invalid parameters or contract violations. | Interview Context: I normally treat 400 as a permanent request/data issue and correct the request rather than retrying indefinitely.
http status 401: HTTP 401 indicates that authentication is missing, invalid or unacceptable to the target service. | Common Causes: Expired token, wrong credentials or incorrect authentication flow. | Interview Context: I verify token acquisition, credentials and scopes before attempting retries.
http status 403: HTTP 403 indicates that the server understood the request but refuses access. | Common Causes: Missing role, scope, policy or network authorization. | Interview Context: I investigate authorization and API policy rather than assuming the credentials themselves are invalid.
http status 404: HTTP 404 indicates that the requested resource or endpoint was not found. | Common Causes: Wrong URL, resource ID or API version. | Interview Context: I validate endpoint configuration and identifiers before treating it as a transient failure.
http status 409: HTTP 409 indicates a conflict with the current state of the target resource. | Common Uses: Duplicate business keys, optimistic concurrency or state conflicts. | Interview Context: I handle 409 according to business semantics and often use it as a signal for idempotent create/update logic.
http status 500: HTTP 500 indicates an internal server error at the target service. | Response: It may be transient, so bounded retry can be appropriate depending on the provider. | Interview Context: I capture the provider response and correlation information and avoid unlimited retries.
http status 502: HTTP 502 indicates a gateway or proxy received an invalid response from an upstream service. | Response: Often transient, but depends on the provider architecture. | Interview Context: I consider retry with backoff while monitoring whether the upstream dependency is consistently failing.
http status 503: HTTP 503 indicates the service is temporarily unavailable or overloaded. | Response: Bounded retry, backoff and queueing can help. | Interview Context: I protect the runtime with retry limits and avoid turning an outage into a retry storm.
http status 504: HTTP 504 indicates a gateway timeout waiting for an upstream service. | Risk: The upstream operation may have completed even though the response timed out. | Interview Context: I combine timeout handling with idempotency before retrying a 504.
api endpoint: An API endpoint is the address and operation through which a consumer interacts with a service. | Capabilities: It can include host, path, method, parameters and authentication requirements. | Interview Context: I treat endpoint details as environment-specific configuration rather than hardcoding them into maps or scripts.
uri: URI is a Uniform Resource Identifier used to identify a resource or endpoint. | API Context: REST APIs commonly use URI paths to represent resources. | Interview Context: I distinguish the URI path from query parameters and from the broader URL when explaining API requests.
url: URL is a Uniform Resource Locator that identifies a network resource and how to access it. | API Context: It commonly combines scheme, host, port, path and optional query parameters. | Interview Context: In Boomi, I keep environment-specific URLs externalized through configuration.
query parameter: A query parameter is a key/value parameter appended to an HTTP request URL to filter, sort or modify a request. | Example: page=1 or status=active. | Interview Context: I validate encoding and provider-specific semantics because query parameters are part of the API contract.
path parameter: A path parameter is a dynamic value embedded in an API URL path, such as /customers/{id}. | Capabilities: Identifies a specific resource or hierarchy. | Interview Context: I distinguish path parameters from query parameters because they have different meanings in the API contract.
http header: An HTTP header carries metadata about a request or response. | Examples: Authorization, Content-Type, Accept, correlation IDs and provider-specific headers. | Interview Context: Headers are often where authentication, content negotiation and tracing information are carried.
content type: Content-Type identifies the media type of an HTTP request or response body. | Examples: application/json and application/xml. | Interview Context: Incorrect Content-Type can cause a valid payload to be rejected by the target API.
accept header: The Accept header tells a server which response media types the client can handle. | Capabilities: Helps negotiate JSON, XML or other representations. | Interview Context: I set it according to the provider API contract rather than assuming the response format.
openapi: OpenAPI is a machine-readable specification format for describing HTTP APIs. | Capabilities: Defines endpoints, methods, parameters, schemas, responses and security requirements. | Interview Context: I use an OpenAPI definition as a contract to understand an API before building the Boomi process.
swagger: Swagger is the commonly used ecosystem name around tools and specifications associated with OpenAPI. | Capabilities: Provides API documentation, testing and design tooling. | Interview Context: When a vendor gives me Swagger/OpenAPI documentation, I use it to understand endpoints, request schemas, responses and authentication.
wsdl: WSDL is an XML-based description of a SOAP web service contract. | Capabilities: Defines operations, messages, bindings and service endpoints. | Interview Context: For SOAP integration I use the WSDL to understand the request/response contract and operation definitions.
schema: A schema defines the expected structure and data types of a document or API payload. | Capabilities: Enables validation and provides structure for transformation. | Interview Context: I treat schema as the contract and mapping as the transformation between contracts.
xsd: XSD is XML Schema Definition, used to formally define the structure and data types of XML documents. | Capabilities: Defines elements, attributes, types, occurrence rules and constraints. | Interview Context: I use XSD-driven profiles when an XML integration requires strict structure or partner validation.
min occurs: minOccurs defines the minimum number of times an XML schema element can occur. | Examples: 0 makes an element optional while 1 generally makes it required. | Interview Context: It matters during XML validation and when mapping required versus optional fields.
max occurs: maxOccurs defines the maximum number of times an XML schema element can occur. | Examples: 1 allows one occurrence while unbounded allows repeated occurrences. | Interview Context: It determines whether Boomi should expect a repeating element and affects mapping structure.
array: An array is an ordered collection of values in JSON or similar data models. | Capabilities: Arrays represent repeating data such as multiple orders or line items. | Interview Context: Repeating JSON arrays often become repeating profile elements and require careful mapping and looping.
json object: A JSON object is a collection of key/value pairs enclosed in braces. | Capabilities: Objects represent structured entities and can contain nested objects and arrays. | Interview Context: I map JSON objects according to their hierarchy rather than treating the payload as a flat list.
json key: A JSON key names a value inside a JSON object. | Capabilities: Keys identify fields such as customerId or status. | Interview Context: The key is part of the API contract and is case-sensitive in many implementations.
flat file: A flat file is a text-based data format where records and fields are represented through delimiters or fixed positions rather than nested markup. | Capabilities: Common forms are CSV, pipe-delimited and fixed-width files. | Interview Context: Flat files are common in legacy and batch integrations, so profile accuracy around delimiters, positions and record types is critical.
csv: CSV is a comma-separated values format commonly used for tabular data exchange. | Capabilities: Represents rows and fields using delimiters and may include quoted values and headers. | Interview Context: I validate quoting, embedded commas, headers, encoding and line endings before assuming a CSV is straightforward.
fixed width: Fixed-width data uses predefined character positions and lengths for each field. | Capabilities: Common in legacy mainframe and batch integrations. | Interview Context: The profile must accurately define start positions and lengths or every downstream field can shift.
record: A record is a logical data unit within a document, such as a database row, flat-file line or business transaction segment. | Capabilities: Records can be split, mapped, validated and routed. | Interview Context: I distinguish a record from a Boomi document because one document can contain multiple business records.
segment: A segment is a logical record in an EDI document, usually containing an identifier followed by elements. | Capabilities: X12 and EDIFACT use segment structures to represent business information. | Interview Context: Segment identifiers and qualifiers determine how Boomi interprets the EDI structure.
element: An element is an individual field within a structured record or EDI segment. | Capabilities: Elements hold business values and may have data types or qualifiers. | Interview Context: In EDI I distinguish segment, element and qualifier because each represents a different level of structure.
composite element: A composite element contains multiple related sub-elements within a single EDI structure. | Capabilities: Allows compact representation of related values. | Interview Context: I verify the partner's EDI profile because composite separators are part of the interchange rules.
trading partner agreement: A Trading Partner Agreement defines the rules for exchanging documents with a business partner. | Capabilities: Can cover identifiers, protocols, security, document standards and acknowledgements. | Interview Context: I treat the agreement as the operational contract that drives partner-specific configuration.
as2: AS2 is a secure B2B protocol commonly used to exchange EDI payloads over HTTP/S. | Capabilities: Supports encryption, signing and Message Disposition Notifications. | Interview Context: In B2B integrations I pay attention to certificates, signatures, encryption and MDN behavior.
mdn: MDN is a Message Disposition Notification used with AS2 to acknowledge receipt and processing disposition of a message at the transport/security layer. | Capabilities: Provides evidence of AS2 message handling. | Interview Context: I distinguish MDN from an EDI functional acknowledgement because they occur at different protocol/business levels.
edi 997: EDI 997 is an X12 Functional Acknowledgement used to indicate whether an interchange or functional group was received and syntactically accepted. | Interview Context: It does not necessarily mean the business transaction was fully processed; I distinguish technical/functional acknowledgement from business acceptance.
edi 999: EDI 999 is an X12 Implementation Acknowledgement used to report syntax and implementation-level validation results. | Interview Context: I use 999 responses to understand whether an inbound EDI transaction met implementation rules, not as proof of business completion.
edi 850: EDI 850 is an X12 Purchase Order transaction. | Interview Context: In an 850 integration I focus on partner-specific envelope rules, order header/line mapping, identifiers, validation and acknowledgement handling.
edi 810: EDI 810 is an X12 Invoice transaction. | Interview Context: Invoice integrations typically require careful mapping of invoice headers, line items, taxes, totals, references and partner-specific requirements.
edi 855: EDI 855 is an X12 Purchase Order Acknowledgement. | Interview Context: It communicates supplier acknowledgement or changes to an order and often maps back to the original purchase order identifiers.
edi 856: EDI 856 is an X12 Advance Ship Notice. | Interview Context: It commonly carries hierarchical shipment, package and item information, so profile hierarchy and identifiers are important.
edi 820: EDI 820 is an X12 Payment Order/Remittance Advice transaction. | Interview Context: Mapping requires careful handling of payment references, amounts, dates and partner-specific segments.
edi 940: EDI 940 is an X12 Warehouse Shipping Order. | Interview Context: It communicates warehouse fulfillment instructions and usually requires partner-specific warehouse, order and line-item mappings.
edi 945: EDI 945 is an X12 Warehouse Shipping Advice. | Interview Context: It communicates shipment completion details back to a trading partner and commonly relates to an originating 940.
master data hub: Boomi Master Data Hub is a master-data management capability for creating governed, trusted records across source systems. | Capabilities: Supports models, repositories, matching, merging, golden records, quarantine and syndication. | Interview Context: I use MDM when the business needs a governed master representation rather than simple system-to-system synchronization.
golden record: A golden record is the trusted master representation of a business entity created from source-system records. | Capabilities: Matching, merging and survivorship rules determine the trusted values. | Interview Context: The goal is not merely to copy data but to establish a consistent business truth.
match rule: A match rule determines when two source records should be considered representations of the same business entity. | Capabilities: Can use exact or configured matching criteria depending on the MDM design. | Interview Context: Poor match rules can merge unrelated customers, so I treat matching as a business-data governance decision.
merge rule: A merge rule determines how multiple matched records are combined into a consolidated master record. | Capabilities: Can determine which source values survive when records disagree. | Interview Context: I explain merge as the decision about how the golden record is constructed after records are identified as the same entity.
survivorship: Survivorship is the rule set that determines which source value becomes the trusted value when multiple records contain different values. | Interview Context: It is a core MDM concept because matching alone identifies duplicates; survivorship determines the resulting golden data.
quarantine: Quarantine isolates records that cannot safely be mastered or processed because they violate data-quality or business rules. | Interview Context: I use quarantine to prevent questionable data from contaminating downstream master data while allowing controlled review.
syndication: Syndication publishes governed master data from the master system to consuming applications. | Interview Context: MDM syndication is different from arbitrary replication because the published value is the governed master representation.
business rule: A Business Rules step evaluates configured business conditions against document data. | Capabilities: Supports decision-making based on rules without embedding all logic in custom scripts. | Interview Context: I prefer maintainable business-rule configuration when the logic is rule-oriented and likely to change.
cleanse: Cleanse is used to standardize or validate data according to configured cleansing rules. | Capabilities: Helps normalize inconsistent source values before downstream matching or mapping. | Interview Context: I use cleansing before mastering or downstream synchronization when source data quality is inconsistent.
lookup: A lookup retrieves a value from a configured reference source during transformation or processing. | Capabilities: Can translate codes or enrich documents without hardcoding every value. | Interview Context: I use lookups for stable reference data and choose CRT, Document Cache or external queries according to the data's lifecycle and volume.
user defined function: A User Defined Function is custom mapping logic packaged for reuse within Maps. | Capabilities: Encapsulates repeated transformation logic and can improve map readability when used appropriately. | Interview Context: I prefer standard functions first and use UDFs when the transformation is genuinely reusable or not practical with built-in functions.
groovy: Groovy is a JVM scripting language that can be used in Boomi scripting scenarios for custom processing. | Capabilities: Provides flexibility for transformations or logic not easily expressed through standard shapes/functions. | Interview Context: I use scripting selectively because excessive custom code reduces maintainability and can complicate support and performance.
javascript: JavaScript can be used in supported Boomi scripting contexts for custom document processing or transformation logic. | Capabilities: Enables custom behavior beyond standard shapes and functions. | Interview Context: I use standard Boomi functionality first and scripting only when it provides a clear benefit.
regular expression: A regular expression is a pattern used to search, validate or transform text. | Capabilities: Useful for extracting IDs, validating formats and replacing text. | Interview Context: I use regex carefully because complex patterns can become hard to maintain and may have performance implications.
null handling: Null handling defines what an integration should do when a source field has no value. | Capabilities: Mapping can default, conditionally populate, omit or transform missing values. | Interview Context: I make null behavior explicit because sending empty values can have different business meaning from omitting a field.
default value: A default value is a fallback value used when a source field is absent or does not meet a condition. | Interview Context: I only apply defaults when the business contract defines a safe default; otherwise I prefer validation and explicit errors.
branch vs route: Branch sends processing into multiple paths, while Route selects a path based on routing conditions. | Interview Context: If all required branches should execute, I consider Branch; if a document should go to one appropriate destination, I consider Route.
decision vs route: Decision is typically suited to evaluating a condition and choosing between defined paths, while Route is designed for broader conditional routing scenarios. | Interview Context: I use the simplest shape that clearly communicates the business decision and keeps the process maintainable.
process route vs process call: Process Call invokes a known reusable subprocess, while Process Route dynamically selects a process based on runtime routing information. | Interview Context: I use Process Call for deliberate reuse and Process Route when routing targets need to be selected or managed dynamically.
try catch vs exception: Try/Catch handles failures and provides an error path, while Exception intentionally creates a failure condition. | Interview Context: I use Exception to stop processing when a business or validation condition is unacceptable, and Try/Catch when I need controlled recovery or error routing.
document error: A document error affects processing of a particular document and can often be isolated so other documents continue. | Interview Context: This is important for batch processing because one invalid record should not automatically cause all valid records to fail.
process error: A process error affects the execution flow itself rather than being limited to one business document. | Causes: Configuration failures, runtime problems, unhandled exceptions or system-level conditions. | Interview Context: Process errors generally require broader operational investigation than an isolated bad document.
business error: A business error means the data or request violates a business rule even if the technical communication succeeded. | Examples: Invalid customer status, unsupported order type or duplicate business transaction. | Interview Context: I handle business errors differently from transient technical failures because retrying bad business data usually will not fix it.
technical error: A technical error results from infrastructure, connectivity, runtime or system behavior rather than invalid business content. | Examples: Timeout, unavailable endpoint, network failure or runtime resource issue. | Interview Context: Technical errors may be transient and therefore candidates for controlled retry.
partial failure: Partial failure occurs when some documents or operations succeed while others fail in the same overall integration execution. | Capabilities: Document-level error handling and tracking allow successful work to continue while failed work is captured. | Interview Context: I design for partial failure rather than assuming a batch is always all-or-nothing.
exactly once: Exactly-once processing is the guarantee that a business effect occurs once even when delivery or execution may be retried. | Reality: End-to-end exactly-once semantics are difficult across independent systems and usually require idempotency or transactional coordination. | Interview Context: I prefer saying 'effectively once through idempotency' rather than promising exactly-once delivery without qualification.
at least once: At-least-once delivery means a message is intended to be delivered one or more times, so duplicates are possible. | Interview Context: Many reliable messaging systems favor at-least-once delivery, making idempotent consumers important.
at most once: At-most-once delivery attempts to avoid duplicates but may lose messages when failures occur. | Interview Context: I choose delivery semantics based on business tolerance for loss versus duplication.
compensation: Compensation is a corrective action that semantically reverses or offsets a previously completed business action when a distributed transaction cannot be rolled back atomically. | Interview Context: I use compensation thinking when integrating independent systems where database-style rollback cannot undo a remote API call.
distributed transaction: A distributed transaction spans multiple independent resources or systems. | Risk: Coordinating atomic commit across APIs, databases and SaaS systems is complex. | Interview Context: I usually design integrations around idempotency, state transitions and compensation rather than assuming a global transaction.
acid: ACID describes database transaction properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability. | Integration Context: ACID applies strongly within a database transaction, but it does not automatically make a multi-system Boomi process atomic. | Interview Context: I use ACID when discussing database reliability and separately discuss distributed integration consistency.
database deadlock: A database deadlock occurs when transactions wait on locks held by each other and neither can proceed. | Response: Investigate transaction order, indexing, batch size and isolation behavior. | Interview Context: Reducing transaction scope and keeping updates ordered consistently can help prevent deadlocks.
database index: A database index accelerates lookups by maintaining an access structure for selected columns. | Integration Context: Indexes on business keys, join columns and delta-load timestamps can significantly improve Boomi query performance. | Interview Context: Before tuning Boomi concurrency, I check whether the database query itself is properly indexed.
primary key: A primary key uniquely identifies a row in a relational table. | Integration Context: It is often used as a stable identifier for updates, joins and idempotency. | Interview Context: I prefer a reliable primary or business key for synchronization rather than matching on unstable descriptive fields.
foreign key: A foreign key references a key in another table and enforces a relational relationship. | Integration Context: Insert/update order can matter when parent and child records have foreign-key dependencies. | Interview Context: I account for parent-child ordering when designing database synchronization.
composite key: A composite key uses multiple fields together to uniquely identify a record. | Integration Context: Useful when no single field uniquely identifies the business entity. | Interview Context: I use the complete key consistently for upsert and idempotency decisions.
cdc: Change Data Capture identifies inserts, updates and deletes from a source system so downstream integrations can process only changes. | Capabilities: Can use database logs, timestamps, sequence values or source-specific mechanisms. | Interview Context: CDC is valuable for high-volume synchronization because it avoids repeatedly extracting unchanged records.
watermark: A watermark is the last successfully processed business or technical position used to implement incremental processing. | Examples: Last modified timestamp, sequence number, database ID or source-system event position. | Interview Answer: Instead of reading the entire source every time, I store the last successful watermark and query only records newer than that value. I update the watermark only after the corresponding business processing succeeds. | Follow-up: Discuss duplicate windows, failure recovery, timestamp precision and where the watermark is persisted.
last run date: Last Run Date is a persisted timestamp or state value used to identify data changed since the previous successful execution. | Capabilities: Supports incremental or delta loads. | Interview Context: I define timezone, precision, overlap and failure semantics carefully so records are not missed at boundary conditions.
reconciliation: Reconciliation compares source and target states to identify missing, extra or inconsistent records. | Capabilities: Supports operational assurance and periodic data-quality checks. | Interview Context: I use reconciliation as a separate control process rather than assuming successful execution means data is fully synchronized.
data validation: Data validation checks whether incoming data satisfies structural, technical and business requirements before downstream processing. | Capabilities: Can include required-field checks, data types, reference values and business rules. | Interview Context: Early validation prevents bad data from creating harder downstream failures.
canonical data model: A canonical data model is a standardized internal representation used to reduce direct transformations between every pair of systems. | Benefit: Can reduce point-to-point mapping complexity when many systems share common business entities. | Interview Context: I use canonical models selectively because they add governance and transformation overhead and are most valuable when many systems share common semantics.
orchestration: Orchestration coordinates a sequence of integration actions and system calls according to a central process. | Capabilities: A Boomi process can orchestrate validation, transformation, enrichment and delivery. | Interview Context: I use orchestration when the integration needs a defined workflow across multiple systems.
choreography: Choreography is an integration style where independent services react to events rather than one central process controlling every step. | Benefit: Can reduce central coupling but increases event and operational complexity. | Interview Context: I consider choreography for event-driven ecosystems where services own their own reactions to business events.
enterprise service bus: An Enterprise Service Bus is an integration architecture pattern that centralizes or standardizes communication, routing, transformation and mediation between systems. | Interview Context: Boomi can fulfill many ESB-like integration responsibilities, but modern architectures may combine APIs and events rather than relying on a traditional centralized bus.
api led connectivity: API-led connectivity organizes integration around reusable APIs commonly described as system, process and experience APIs. | Benefit: Promotes reusable interfaces and decouples consumers from backend implementations. | Interview Context: I use API-led thinking when multiple consumers need governed access to common business capabilities.
system api: A System API exposes access to a core system without exposing all implementation details to consumers. | Interview Context: It can standardize access to databases, ERPs or SaaS systems and isolate backend changes.
process api: A Process API combines or orchestrates data from one or more systems into a reusable business capability. | Interview Context: It separates business orchestration from individual system connectivity.
experience api: An Experience API tailors a business capability for a specific consumer or channel. | Interview Context: It can shape a common process capability for mobile, web or partner-specific needs without changing the underlying system API.
loose coupling: Loose coupling minimizes direct dependency between communicating systems so one side can change or fail with less impact on the other. | Capabilities: APIs, queues, events and canonical contracts can help. | Interview Context: I use loose coupling when independent lifecycle, scaling or failure behavior is important.
tight coupling: Tight coupling means two systems depend strongly on each other's availability, timing or implementation details. | Risk: Changes and outages propagate more directly. | Interview Context: Synchronous point-to-point integrations are often more tightly coupled than asynchronous event-based patterns.
stateless: A stateless integration does not depend on previous execution state to process the current request. | Benefit: Easier scaling and failover because any capable runtime can process the request. | Interview Context: I prefer stateless APIs where possible and externalize required state into durable systems.
stateful: A stateful integration depends on stored information from previous processing to determine current behavior. | Examples: Last-run timestamps, sequence offsets and conversation state. | Interview Context: Stateful designs require careful persistence, consistency and recovery considerations.
blocking: Blocking processing waits for an operation to complete before continuing. | Integration Context: Synchronous API/database calls can block threads while waiting for downstream responses. | Interview Context: Excessive blocking under high concurrency can exhaust runtime threads.
non blocking: Non-blocking processing allows other work to progress without waiting synchronously for a long-running operation. | Integration Context: Asynchronous queues and event-driven patterns can reduce blocking dependencies. | Interview Context: I use asynchronous architecture when downstream latency should not tie up producer processing.
scalability: Scalability is the ability of an integration solution to handle increased workload by adding or increasing capacity. | Types: Horizontal scaling adds nodes; vertical scaling increases resources per node. | Interview Context: I measure workload growth, bottlenecks and downstream constraints before choosing a scaling strategy.
horizontal scaling: Horizontal scaling increases capacity by adding runtime nodes or processing workers. | Benefit: Can improve capacity and resilience when the architecture supports distributed execution. | Interview Context: Runtime clusters are the natural Boomi architecture to discuss for horizontal execution capacity.
vertical scaling: Vertical scaling increases CPU, memory or other resources available to an existing runtime node. | Benefit: Can help resource-heavy workloads but has physical or infrastructure limits. | Interview Context: I use vertical scaling when the workload is resource constrained and horizontal distribution is not sufficient or practical.
resilience: Resilience is the ability of an integration system to continue operating or recover predictably when components fail. | Capabilities: Retry, timeout, circuit-breaker-like controls, queues, idempotency and failover contribute to resilience. | Interview Context: I design resilience around expected failure modes rather than simply adding retries everywhere.
circuit breaker: A circuit breaker is a resilience pattern that temporarily stops calls to a failing dependency to prevent cascading failure. | Integration Context: It is commonly implemented in API gateways, application layers or custom integration architectures depending on platform capabilities. | Interview Context: When a downstream service is repeatedly unavailable, stopping new calls can be safer than creating a retry storm.
retry storm: A retry storm occurs when many failed requests are retried simultaneously and create even more load on an already failing dependency. | Prevention: Exponential/backoff delays, jitter, bounded retries and queues. | Interview Context: I always consider aggregate retry volume, not just retry count per document.
exponential backoff: Exponential backoff increases the delay between repeated retry attempts. | Benefit: Reduces pressure on temporarily unavailable services and spreads retries over time. | Interview Context: I combine backoff with a retry limit and provider guidance such as Retry-After.
jitter: Jitter adds controlled randomness to retry delays so many workers do not retry at exactly the same moment. | Benefit: Helps prevent synchronized retry spikes. | Interview Context: It is useful in distributed systems with many concurrent workers.
observability: Observability is the ability to understand system behavior from telemetry such as logs, metrics and traces. | Integration Context: Correlation IDs, execution records, timings, error details and business identifiers improve Boomi observability. | Interview Context: Good observability reduces mean time to detect and resolve production incidents.
correlation id: A Correlation ID is a unique identifier used to trace one business transaction across multiple integration steps and systems. | Core Use: It connects inbound requests, logs, downstream calls, retries and responses into one traceable transaction. | Interview Answer: I generate or preserve a correlation ID at the entry point and carry it through document properties, logs and downstream requests. This is one of the most useful tools for production troubleshooting. | Follow-up: Explain where you store it, how it survives branching and how support uses it during RCA.
transaction id: A Transaction ID identifies a particular business or technical transaction. | Capabilities: Useful for deduplication, tracking and reconciliation. | Interview Context: I distinguish transaction ID from correlation ID: transaction ID identifies the transaction, while correlation ID often groups related calls across systems.
business key: A business key is a domain-specific identifier that uniquely or meaningfully identifies a business entity or transaction. | Examples: Order number, customer number or invoice number. | Interview Context: Business keys are central to idempotency, reconciliation and update logic.
secret: A secret is sensitive information such as a password, API key, token or private key. | Security: Secrets should be protected through supported credential/configuration mechanisms and never hardcoded into process scripts or payloads unnecessarily. | Interview Context: I treat secrets as configuration and apply least privilege and rotation practices.
least privilege: Least privilege means granting only the access required to perform a task. | Security Context: Applies to Boomi users, runtime service accounts, database users and API credentials. | Interview Context: It limits blast radius if an identity is compromised.
credential: A credential is information used to authenticate to a system, such as a username/password, token, key or certificate. | Integration Context: Credentials should be externalized and protected from source code and logs. | Interview Context: I also verify that credentials are not accidentally exposed through error messages or debug logging.
truststore: A truststore contains trusted certificates used to validate remote certificates during TLS connections. | Integration Context: It is important for HTTPS and other certificate-based connections when the remote CA is not already trusted. | Interview Context: A trust failure often means the runtime does not trust the server certificate chain.
keystore: A keystore contains private keys and certificates used by a client or server for identity and cryptographic operations. | Integration Context: Common in mTLS and client-certificate authentication. | Interview Context: I distinguish keystore from truststore: keystore represents our identity/private keys, truststore represents identities we trust.
certificate chain: A certificate chain links a leaf certificate through intermediate authorities to a trusted root CA. | Integration Context: All required intermediates may need to be available for successful validation. | Interview Context: A certificate can be unexpired yet still fail because its chain is incomplete or untrusted.
root ca: A Root Certificate Authority is a trusted authority at the top of a certificate trust chain. | Capabilities: Its trust establishes the basis for validating subordinate certificates. | Interview Context: Truststore configuration often determines whether the runtime trusts a remote certificate chain.
private key: A private key is secret cryptographic material used for signing, decryption or client authentication depending on the protocol. | Security: It must never be shared publicly or logged. | Interview Context: In SFTP it can authenticate the client; in TLS it can represent client identity for mTLS.
public key: A public key is the shareable counterpart to a private key used for verification or encryption depending on the cryptographic scheme. | Integration Context: SSH and TLS certificates rely on public/private key concepts. | Interview Context: Public key distribution is not the same as sharing the private key.
ssh: SSH is a secure protocol used for encrypted remote communication and authentication. | SFTP Context: SFTP operates over SSH and commonly uses port 22. | Interview Context: I distinguish the SSH transport/security layer from the SFTP file-transfer protocol built on it.
ftp: FTP is the traditional File Transfer Protocol used to transfer files between systems. | Security: Basic FTP does not encrypt credentials or payloads in transit. | Interview Context: I prefer SFTP or FTPS when secure transport is required.
ftps: FTPS is FTP secured with TLS. | Difference: It uses FTP plus TLS rather than SSH-based SFTP. | Interview Context: SFTP and FTPS are both secure file-transfer choices but use different underlying protocols and configuration models.
scp: SCP is a secure file-copy protocol built around SSH. | Difference: It is focused on copying files rather than providing the broader SFTP file-operation model. | Interview Context: I choose based on the partner protocol and required file operations.
ssh host key: An SSH host key helps the client verify the identity of the remote SSH server. | Security Context: It protects against connecting to an unexpected or malicious server. | Interview Context: I treat host-key verification separately from user authentication because both server trust and client identity matter.
file archive: File archiving moves successfully processed source files to a controlled archive location instead of leaving them in the active input directory. | Benefits: Supports auditability and duplicate prevention. | Interview Context: I prefer deterministic post-processing such as move/archive after successful completion and retain failed files for investigation.
file naming convention: A file naming convention is a predictable pattern for identifying files by business date, partner, transaction type or sequence. | Capabilities: Enables filtering, routing and operational troubleshooting. | Interview Context: Good naming conventions make polling and duplicate detection easier.
file encoding: File encoding defines how characters are represented as bytes, such as UTF-8 or another character set. | Risk: Incorrect encoding can corrupt special characters or cause parsing errors. | Interview Context: I verify source encoding when files contain non-ASCII data.
line ending: A line ending marks the boundary between text records and varies across operating systems. | Integration Context: CRLF and LF differences can affect flat-file parsing or downstream systems. | Interview Context: When a file behaves differently across environments, I check line endings along with delimiter and encoding.
gzip: GZIP is a compression format used to reduce file size during storage or transfer. | Integration Context: Boomi file/API processing may encounter compressed payloads depending on the connector and configuration. | Interview Context: Compression reduces network usage but adds CPU processing and requires compatible decompression behavior.
base64: Base64 is an encoding scheme that represents binary data as text. | Integration Context: Commonly used for binary payloads, attachments or credentials within APIs, but it is not encryption. | Interview Context: I explicitly distinguish Base64 encoding from encryption because Base64 provides no confidentiality.
encryption at rest: Encryption at rest protects stored data on disks or databases from unauthorized access. | Security Context: Applies to persisted payloads, credentials, logs and external storage depending on architecture. | Interview Context: I distinguish it from TLS, which protects data in transit.
encryption in transit: Encryption in transit protects data while it moves between systems, commonly using TLS or SSH. | Interview Context: HTTPS and SFTP are examples of secure transport, but they do not by themselves determine authorization or business-level data protection.
rbac: Role-Based Access Control grants permissions through roles rather than assigning every permission individually to every user. | Benefit: Simplifies governance and supports least privilege. | Interview Context: I use RBAC for Boomi platform administration and deployment separation.
code review: Code review is peer examination of integration logic, configuration and implementation before release. | Integration Context: Review should cover error handling, security, performance, naming, reuse and maintainability. | Interview Context: As a lead, I focus on whether the process is correct, supportable and production-safe rather than only whether it works on the happy path.
unit testing: Unit testing verifies a small, isolated piece of logic. | Integration Context: Map functions, reusable logic and custom scripts can be unit-tested conceptually or through automated test approaches. | Interview Context: Unit testing is different from end-to-end integration testing because it isolates a smaller behavior.
integration testing: Integration testing verifies communication and behavior between multiple components or systems. | Integration Context: Tests include real or controlled endpoints, schemas, authentication and error conditions. | Interview Context: I use it to validate that Boomi and the target system work together correctly.
regression testing: Regression testing verifies that existing functionality still works after a change. | Integration Context: Shared maps, subprocesses and connectors make regression testing especially important in Boomi because one change can affect multiple processes. | Interview Context: I prioritize impacted interfaces and reusable dependencies in regression testing.
sit: System Integration Testing verifies that integrated systems work together according to the overall solution design. | Interview Context: SIT should cover positive, negative, boundary and error-handling scenarios across system boundaries.
uat: User Acceptance Testing validates that the solution meets business requirements from the user's perspective. | Interview Context: Technical success is not enough; UAT confirms business outcomes, mappings and operational behavior.
incident: An incident is an unplanned event that causes or risks service disruption or incorrect processing. | Production Context: Incident response focuses first on restoring safe service and limiting business impact. | Interview Context: I separate immediate incident handling from later root-cause and preventive actions.
problem management: Problem management identifies and addresses underlying causes of recurring incidents. | Capabilities: Includes trend analysis, RCA and permanent corrective actions. | Interview Context: If the same SFTP or API failure keeps recurring, I treat it as a problem-management issue rather than repeatedly resolving incidents manually.
change request: A change request formally records a modification to an integration, configuration or infrastructure. | Capabilities: Supports impact assessment, approval, testing and release traceability. | Interview Context: Production changes should be controlled and auditable.
hotfix: A hotfix is an urgent targeted change released to address a production defect or critical issue. | Risk: Speed must be balanced with testing and rollback planning. | Interview Context: I use the smallest safe change possible and follow emergency-release controls where applicable.
rollback: Rollback restores a previously known-good version or configuration after a failed release. | Capabilities: Requires versioning, deployment traceability and a defined recovery procedure. | Interview Context: I plan rollback before production deployment rather than designing it only after a failure.
blue green deployment: Blue/Green deployment maintains two environments or versions so traffic or execution can shift from the current version to the new version with reduced interruption. | Integration Context: Applicability depends on runtime and deployment architecture. | Interview Context: I use the pattern when the infrastructure supports controlled cutover and rollback.
canary deployment: Canary deployment releases a change to a small portion of traffic or workload before broader rollout. | Benefit: Limits blast radius and provides early production feedback. | Interview Context: It is useful when traffic can be partitioned and the runtime architecture supports gradual rollout.
dev test prod: DEV, TEST/UAT and PROD are common lifecycle environments used to separate development, validation and live processing. | Capabilities: Environment Extensions allow environment-specific endpoints and credentials without changing core logic. | Interview Context: I promote tested components forward and avoid editing production code directly.
agile sprint: A sprint is a fixed iteration in Agile delivery during which a team plans and completes a set of work. | Integration Context: Integration dependencies, API readiness, test data and environment availability often affect sprint delivery. | Interview Context: I raise external dependencies early rather than discovering them during UAT.
backlog: A backlog is an ordered collection of work items such as stories, defects and technical tasks. | Integration Context: It can include interfaces, mappings, production fixes and technical debt. | Interview Context: I prioritize work based on business value, risk and dependencies.
user story: A user story describes a desired capability from a user's or business perspective. | Integration Context: A good integration story includes source, target, business event, data, expected outcome and acceptance criteria. | Interview Context: I clarify ambiguous integration requirements before design begins.
acceptance criteria: Acceptance criteria define the conditions that must be true for a requirement to be considered complete. | Integration Context: Include successful flows, validation, error handling, performance and security expectations where relevant. | Interview Context: Clear acceptance criteria reduce mapping and interpretation disputes later.
definition of done: Definition of Done is the team's agreed checklist for considering work complete. | Integration Context: It may include code review, testing, documentation, deployment readiness and monitoring. | Interview Context: For integration work I include operational readiness, not just process development.
rca: RCA stands for Root Cause Analysis and identifies why a production issue occurred and what prevents recurrence. | Method: Evidence, timeline, causal chain, corrective action and preventive action. | Interview Context: A good RCA identifies the actual failure mechanism rather than blaming a symptom.
mttr: MTTR is Mean Time To Recovery or Repair, a measure of how quickly incidents are restored depending on the organization's definition. | Interview Context: Better monitoring, runbooks, automation and safe reprocessing can reduce MTTR.
mttd: MTTD is Mean Time To Detect, measuring how long it takes to identify a failure or incident. | Interview Context: Monitoring, alerts and meaningful correlation IDs reduce MTTD.
sla: SLA is a Service Level Agreement defining measurable service expectations such as availability or response time. | Integration Context: Integration design should reflect SLA requirements for latency, throughput and recovery. | Interview Context: I translate SLA requirements into architecture and monitoring metrics.
rto: RTO is Recovery Time Objective, the target time within which service should be restored after a disruption. | Interview Context: RTO influences redundancy, recovery procedures and operational readiness.
rpo: RPO is Recovery Point Objective, the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time or recoverable state. | Interview Context: RPO influences persistence, queueing, backup and replay strategy.
disaster recovery: Disaster Recovery is the planned ability to restore integration services after a major infrastructure or site failure. | Capabilities: Includes runtime recovery, configuration backup, deployment automation, data recovery and tested procedures. | Interview Context: HA handles normal component failures; DR addresses larger failures and recovery objectives.
business continuity: Business Continuity is the broader capability to continue critical business operations during disruptions. | Integration Context: Includes people, processes, infrastructure, dependencies and recovery plans. | Interview Context: Integration architecture contributes to continuity but cannot guarantee it alone.
network connectivity: Network connectivity is the ability of the runtime to reach required endpoints and ports. | Capabilities: Includes DNS, routing, firewall rules, proxies, VPN/private links and TLS. | Interview Context: Many integration failures are connectivity problems, so I validate network path before changing process logic.
firewall: A firewall controls network traffic between systems based on rules such as source, destination and port. | Integration Context: On-prem Boomi runtimes often require outbound or inbound firewall rules for partner and cloud connectivity. | Interview Context: I verify the runtime's network path and required ports before troubleshooting application-level failures.
proxy: A proxy is an intermediary network service through which HTTP or other traffic is routed. | Integration Context: Enterprise environments may require outbound API traffic to use a proxy. | Interview Context: Proxy configuration can cause connectivity failures even when the target endpoint itself is healthy.
dns: DNS translates hostnames into network addresses. | Integration Context: A runtime may fail to connect when DNS resolution is incorrect or unavailable even though the endpoint is operational. | Interview Context: I check DNS, port reachability and TLS separately when troubleshooting connectivity.
port: A port identifies a network service endpoint on a host. | Common Examples: HTTPS commonly uses 443 and SFTP commonly uses 22, though deployments can use different ports. | Interview Context: I verify the actual partner port rather than assuming the default.
tcp: TCP is a connection-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable ordered byte delivery. | Integration Context: Many application protocols such as HTTPS and SFTP operate over TCP. | Interview Context: TCP reliability does not guarantee application-level success.
http: HTTP is the application protocol underlying many web APIs. | Capabilities: Defines methods, headers, status codes and message semantics. | Interview Context: Understanding HTTP helps diagnose Boomi API failures beyond simply reading the connector error.
https: HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS to provide encrypted transport and server identity validation. | Interview Context: HTTPS protects data in transit but still requires correct API authentication and authorization.
soap fault: A SOAP Fault is a structured XML error response returned by a SOAP service. | Capabilities: Provides fault codes and details according to SOAP semantics. | Interview Context: I distinguish SOAP Fault from transport-level HTTP errors because both can represent different failure layers.
api versioning: API versioning manages contract changes so existing consumers are not unexpectedly broken. | Approaches: URI, header or media-type versioning depending on the API design. | Interview Context: I prefer explicit compatibility strategy and controlled deprecation over silently changing a live contract.
backward compatibility: Backward compatibility means a new version continues to support existing consumers or data contracts. | Integration Context: Important when shared APIs, profiles or schemas are used by multiple interfaces. | Interview Context: I assess consumers before changing a shared contract.
schema evolution: Schema evolution is the controlled modification of data structures over time. | Strategies: Add optional fields, version contracts or support old and new schemas during migration. | Interview Context: I avoid breaking consumers by making compatible changes where possible.
contract first: Contract-first integration defines the API or message contract before implementation. | Capabilities: Clarifies request/response structures, errors, security and compatibility expectations. | Interview Context: I prefer contract-first for shared APIs because it aligns producers and consumers before development.
data mapping: Data mapping defines how fields from a source structure correspond to fields in a target structure. | Capabilities: Includes direct mappings, functions, lookups, defaults and conditional logic. | Interview Context: I validate business meaning, not just field names, because two fields with similar names may have different semantics.
data enrichment: Data enrichment adds information to a document from another source. | Examples: Reference lookup, customer master data or external API information. | Interview Context: I consider cache or batch lookup strategies when enrichment would otherwise create one external call per document.
data normalization: Data normalization standardizes values into a consistent representation. | Examples: Date formats, country codes, phone numbers and status values. | Interview Context: I normalize data at a controlled boundary so downstream systems receive predictable values.
data validation rule: A data validation rule checks a document against a defined structural or business requirement. | Capabilities: Required fields, allowed values, ranges and relationships can be validated. | Interview Context: Validation should happen early enough to prevent invalid data from reaching downstream systems.
dead letter pattern: The Dead Letter pattern moves messages that cannot be processed safely into a separate controlled destination. | Benefits: Prevents poison messages from blocking healthy work and preserves evidence for reprocessing. | Interview Context: I combine DLQ with alerting, retention, ownership and a replay procedure.
replay: Replay is deliberate reprocessing of previously captured data after a failure or correction. | Requirements: Preserve original payload, metadata and business identifiers and ensure downstream effects are idempotent. | Interview Context: A replay mechanism is part of production readiness for important integrations.
checkpoint: A checkpoint records progress during long-running or large-volume processing so work can resume from a known point. | Examples: Last processed ID, timestamp, page cursor or file marker. | Interview Context: Checkpoint design reduces the need to restart an entire large workload after a partial failure.
restartability: Restartability is the ability to resume processing safely after interruption without redoing harmful work or losing records. | Capabilities: Uses checkpoints, idempotency, durable state and controlled retry/replay. | Interview Context: I design restartability explicitly for large files and high-volume batch integrations.
data lineage: Data lineage describes where data originated, how it was transformed and where it was delivered. | Capabilities: Tracking IDs, logs, mappings and metadata support lineage. | Interview Context: Lineage is valuable for audit, troubleshooting and regulatory reporting.
audit trail: An audit trail records relevant changes, executions, deployments or business events for traceability. | Integration Context: Production support and regulated processes may require deployment and processing history. | Interview Context: I ensure audit requirements are considered without logging sensitive payload data unnecessarily.
pii: PII is Personally Identifiable Information that can identify or relate to an individual. | Security Context: Integration logs, error payloads and monitoring data should avoid exposing unnecessary PII. | Interview Context: I apply data minimization and masking when sensitive business data enters operational logs.
data masking: Data masking hides or transforms sensitive values so they are not exposed in logs, test environments or operational views. | Interview Context: I mask credentials and sensitive business fields while preserving enough information for troubleshooting.
data retention: Data retention defines how long payloads, logs, files or operational records should be kept. | Integration Context: Retention must balance audit, troubleshooting, storage cost and privacy requirements. | Interview Context: I define retention according to business and compliance requirements rather than keeping everything forever.
multi tenant: Multi-tenancy means shared infrastructure serves multiple logically isolated customers or accounts. | Integration Context: Managed cloud services commonly use tenant isolation while sharing underlying infrastructure. | Interview Context: I distinguish multi-tenant infrastructure from single-tenant runtime deployment because isolation and resource behavior differ.
single tenant: Single tenancy means a runtime or infrastructure instance is dedicated to one customer/account. | Integration Context: Basic Runtime and Runtime Cluster concepts are single-tenant execution models. | Interview Context: Single tenancy can provide stronger resource and network isolation but may require more infrastructure management.
resource isolation: Resource isolation prevents one workload or tenant from consuming resources in a way that destabilizes others. | Capabilities: Separate JVMs, runtime nodes and controlled concurrency can provide isolation. | Interview Context: Forked execution is one mechanism I would discuss when process-level JVM isolation is required.
shared file system: A shared file system allows multiple runtime nodes to access common files and directories. | Integration Context: Legacy clustered runtime architectures may rely on shared storage for coordinated operation. | Interview Context: Shared storage availability and performance become part of the cluster architecture and must be designed carefully.
nfs: NFS is a Network File System protocol that allows systems to access files over a network. | Integration Context: Older clustered runtime architectures may use shared NFS storage for files that must be accessible across nodes. | Interview Context: NFS itself can become a dependency or bottleneck, so I evaluate availability and latency.
queue management: Queue management controls how asynchronous work is stored, consumed, retried and monitored. | Capabilities: Includes concurrency, ordering, retry, dead-letter handling and retention. | Interview Context: I use queue management to smooth spikes and isolate downstream outages while maintaining operational visibility.
message ordering: Message ordering defines whether consumers must process messages in the same sequence in which they were produced. | Risk: Parallel processing can break order unless the messaging design preserves it. | Interview Context: I clarify whether ordering is a true business requirement before sacrificing throughput for sequential processing.
fifo: FIFO means First In, First Out and preserves message ordering within the scope supported by the messaging system. | Interview Context: FIFO is useful when business events must be processed sequentially, but it can reduce parallelism.
message retention: Message retention defines how long a message remains available in a queue or stream for consumption or replay. | Interview Context: Retention should reflect recovery, replay and storage requirements.
consumer scaling: Consumer scaling increases the number of processing workers consuming messages from a queue or stream. | Benefit: Improves throughput when the workload is parallelizable and downstream systems can handle the load. | Interview Context: Scaling consumers without checking target limits can simply move the bottleneck downstream.
load testing: Load testing measures integration behavior under expected or peak workload. | Metrics: Throughput, latency, error rate, CPU, memory and downstream resource usage. | Interview Context: I test realistic payloads and dependencies rather than using only synthetic happy-path data.
stress testing: Stress testing pushes the integration beyond expected load to identify failure thresholds and recovery behavior. | Interview Context: It helps establish safe operating limits and exposes bottlenecks before production.
soak testing: Soak testing runs a workload for an extended period to identify memory leaks, resource exhaustion or gradual degradation. | Interview Context: It is valuable for long-running runtimes and high-volume integrations.
performance bottleneck: A performance bottleneck is the component limiting overall throughput or latency. | Common Causes: Slow API, database query, connector connection pool, runtime CPU/memory, excessive mapping or concurrency. | Interview Context: I measure each stage before optimizing instead of assuming Boomi is the bottleneck.
n plus one query: The N+1 query problem occurs when one query retrieves a list and then one additional database/API call is made for each returned document. | Risk: Produces excessive calls and poor performance. | Interview Context: I avoid it through joins, bulk queries, Document Cache or batched reference data.
batch size: Batch size is the number of records or documents grouped into one processing or database operation. | Tradeoff: Larger batches can improve throughput but increase memory, transaction duration and failure scope. | Interview Context: I tune batch size empirically based on payload size, target limits and recovery requirements.
database commit: A database commit makes a transaction's changes durable. | Integration Context: Commit frequency affects performance, lock duration and failure scope. | Interview Context: I balance batch commits for throughput with restartability and transaction size.
database rollback: A database rollback discards uncommitted changes in a database transaction. | Integration Context: It applies to the database transaction scope and does not automatically undo calls already made to unrelated systems. | Interview Context: I clearly define transaction boundaries in multi-system integrations.
transaction isolation: Transaction isolation controls how concurrently executing database transactions can observe each other's changes. | Integration Context: Isolation affects locking, consistency and concurrency. | Interview Context: I consider database-specific defaults and workload characteristics rather than changing isolation blindly.
sql injection: SQL injection is an attack in which untrusted input alters SQL command meaning. | Security: Use parameterized queries or safe connector mechanisms rather than concatenating untrusted values into SQL. | Interview Context: I treat dynamic SQL carefully and never trust incoming business data as executable SQL.
input validation: Input validation checks incoming values before they are used by downstream systems or security-sensitive operations. | Capabilities: Protects data quality and reduces injection or contract errors. | Interview Context: Validation belongs near trust boundaries, before dangerous operations.
api pagination token: A pagination token or continuation token tells the client how to request the next page of an API result. | Interview Context: Tokens are usually opaque and should be passed back according to provider rules rather than parsed unless explicitly documented.
oauth client credentials: Client Credentials is an OAuth 2.0 flow for machine-to-machine access where an application authenticates as itself. | Interview Context: It is common for server-to-server integrations because there is no interactive end user.
oauth authorization code: Authorization Code is an OAuth 2.0 flow where an application obtains authorization through a user or authorization server and exchanges a code for tokens. | Interview Context: It is common when access is delegated on behalf of a user.
refresh token: A refresh token is a credential used to obtain a new access token without repeating the full authorization interaction when the provider supports refresh tokens. | Security: It must be protected like a secret. | Interview Context: I verify provider-specific expiration, rotation and storage behavior.
oauth scope: An OAuth scope limits what an access token is authorized to access. | Interview Context: A successful token request does not guarantee access to every endpoint; the required scopes must be granted.
basic authentication: Basic Authentication sends a username and password using a base64-encoded HTTP Authorization value, normally over HTTPS. | Security: Base64 is not encryption, so TLS is essential. | Interview Context: I prefer stronger provider-supported authentication when available.
api gateway rate limit: An API gateway rate limit restricts incoming consumer requests to protect backend services and enforce usage policies. | Interview Context: Gateway limits should be aligned with backend capacity and documented consumer expectations.
developer portal: A Developer Portal provides API consumers with documentation, discovery, subscription or access-management capabilities depending on the API management product. | Interview Context: It separates API consumer experience from internal integration implementation.
api policy: An API policy is a reusable governance rule applied to API traffic. | Examples: Authentication, rate limiting, transformation, IP restrictions or headers depending on the gateway. | Interview Context: Policies keep cross-cutting API controls outside individual backend processes.
api consumer: An API consumer is an application, partner or client that calls an exposed API. | Capabilities: Consumers may require credentials, subscriptions, scopes and usage limits. | Interview Context: I design API contracts around consumer needs while protecting backend systems.
api provider: An API provider owns and exposes an API contract to consumers. | Responsibilities: Defines endpoints, schemas, authentication, availability and lifecycle policies. | Interview Context: In an enterprise architecture, Boomi may act as an API provider, consumer or both.
